Name: Garden of Eden
Description: The garden God planted as humanity's first home, where Adam and Eve walked with Him. Four rivers watered it, and at its center stood the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
BiblicalSignificance: Eden is where humanity's story begins - and where it broke. Yet even in the curse, God promised a coming offspring who would crush the serpent: the first whisper of the hope this blog is named for.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Fall; Cain Murders Abel

Name: Mount Ararat
Description: The mountainous region where Noah's ark came to rest as the floodwaters receded, and Noah stepped out into a washed world with his family and every living creature.
BiblicalSignificance: Ararat marks God's judgment and His mercy in the same place: the old world washed away, and a rainbow covenant promising He would never do it again. Every ending with God carries a new beginning.

Name: Babel
Description: The plain in Shinar where humanity built a city and a tower reaching to the heavens, defying God's command to fill the earth. God confused their language and scattered them across the world.
BiblicalSignificance: Babel shows what happens when people chase greatness without God: confusion and scattering. At Pentecost God reversed Babel, uniting every language in one gospel.

Name: Ur
Description: A wealthy Sumerian city of moon-god worship where Abraham was born. God called him out of Ur to a land He would show him - the beginning of the journey of faith.
BiblicalSignificance: Ur represents everything Abraham had to leave: security, family gods, the known. Hope anchored in Christ often starts the same way - leaving the familiar at God's word.

Name: Haran
Description: The Mesopotamian trading city where Abraham settled after leaving Ur, staying until his father Terah died. Generations later Jacob fled here to Laban's household and met Rachel at its well.
BiblicalSignificance: Haran was a halfway stop - obedience begun but not finished. God waited until Abraham moved on. Partial obedience still leaves us short of the promise.

Name: Canaan
ModernLocation: Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, and western Jordan and Syria
Description: The land God promised to Abraham and his descendants - 'a land flowing with milk and honey.' Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived there as nomads, dwelling in tents on the strength of a promise.
BiblicalSignificance: Canaan taught the patriarchs to live as strangers holding a promise. Hebrews says they were looking for a better country - a heavenly one. Our anchor, like theirs, rests in a homeland we have not reached yet.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Name: Shechem
Description: One of the first places Abraham camped in Canaan, where God appeared and promised the land to his offspring. Centuries later Joshua renewed the covenant here, and Joseph's bones were finally buried at Shechem.
BiblicalSignificance: Shechem was a place of altars and choices: Abraham's altar, Jacob's purging of idols, Joshua's 'choose this day whom you will serve.'
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Jacob; Joshua; Joseph, Son of Jacob

Name: Bethel
Description: Where Jacob dreamed of a stairway between heaven and earth, angels ascending and descending, and woke declaring 'Surely the Lord is in this place.' He named it Bethel - house of God.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethel is where a runaway met God in the dark. Jacob arrived with nothing and left with a promise. Jesus later told Nathanael he would see heaven opened - the stairway was a person all along.

Name: Hebron
Description: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth, where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah - his first owned parcel of the promised land. David was anointed king here before taking Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Hebron holds the tombs of the patriarchs: a city of burial that speaks of promise. Abraham owned only a grave there, yet believed his descendants would own it all.

Name: Beersheba
Description: The southernmost city of settled Israel - 'from Dan to Beersheba' marked the nation's full extent. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree here and called on the name of the Lord, the Eternal God.
BiblicalSignificance: Beersheba means 'well of the oath.' The patriarchs kept digging wells and making covenants here, learning that God's promises hold even at the desert's edge.

Name: Egypt
Description: The Nile civilization where Joseph rose from prisoner to prime minister, where Israel multiplied into a nation - and where Pharaoh enslaved them for 400 years.
BiblicalSignificance: Egypt is Scripture's great picture of bondage - and of deliverance. The Exodus became Israel's defining story: our God hears, He comes down, and He brings out. Every redemption since echoes it.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Passover; The Ten Plagues; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Name: Goshen
Description: The fertile delta region Pharaoh gave to Joseph's family - the best of the land. Israel lived here for generations, growing from a family into a people, until Goshen's plenty became Egypt's prison.
BiblicalSignificance: Goshen shows how blessing can curdle into bondage when we settle for less than God's promise. Comfort in Egypt is still Egypt.

Name: Midian
Description: The desert wilderness east of the Red Sea where Moses fled after killing an Egyptian. He shepherded Jethro's flocks here for 40 years until God met him in the burning bush.
BiblicalSignificance: Midian was Moses's school of obscurity - 40 years of silence before the call. God often anchors hope in us during the years nobody sees.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Gideon's Victory over Midian

Name: Mount Sinai
Description: The mountain of God, wrapped in thunder and smoke, where Moses received the Ten Commandments and Israel became a covenant nation.
BiblicalSignificance: Sinai reveals God's holiness - the mountain no one could touch. But the law given there was a tutor leading to Christ, showing us our need for the grace that would come.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Golden Calf; The Burning Bush

Name: Kadesh Barnea
Description: The wilderness camp where the twelve spies returned from Canaan. Ten brought fear, two brought faith - and Israel's unbelief turned an eleven-day journey into forty years of wandering.
BiblicalSignificance: Kadesh Barnea is the geography of almost. A whole generation stood at the edge of promise and turned back. Hope anchored in Christ refuses to let fear veto God's promise.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief; Wilderness Wanderings

Name: Jordan River
Description: The river Israel crossed on dry ground to enter the promised land, its waters piled up as the priests' feet touched them. Centuries later John baptized in the Jordan, and Jesus Himself was baptized here.
BiblicalSignificance: The Jordan is Scripture's river of transition - from wilderness to promise, from old life to new. Every crossing says the same thing: God makes a way through.
RelatedPeople: Joshua; Elijah; Elisha; John the Baptist; Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; Crossing the Jordan

Name: Plains of Moab
ModernLocation: Jordan, east of the Dead Sea
Description: The final camp of the wilderness generation, across the Jordan from Jericho. Here Moses preached Deuteronomy, viewed the promised land from Mount Nebo, and died.
BiblicalSignificance: The plains of Moab are where one generation ended and another began - Moses's farewell sermons handing the promise to those who would actually enter it.

Name: Jericho
Description: The fortified Canaanite city whose walls fell after Israel marched around them for seven days - the first conquest of the promised land. Later, Jesus healed blind Bartimaeus and called Zacchaeus down from his tree here.
BiblicalSignificance: Jericho proves that God's battle plans rarely look like ours. Marching, trumpets, and a shout - and the walls fell. Victory belongs to the Lord, not to conventional wisdom.

Name: Gilgal
Description: Israel's first camp inside the promised land, where twelve stones from the Jordan were set up as a memorial, the manna ceased, and the nation celebrated its first Passover in Canaan.
BiblicalSignificance: Gilgal was Israel's memorial ground - stones of remembrance for a generation prone to forget. Remembering what God has done anchors hope for what He will do.

Name: Ai
Description: The small city that humiliated Israel after the triumph at Jericho - defeated because of Achan's hidden sin, then taken after the sin was judged.
BiblicalSignificance: Ai teaches that hidden sin stops a whole people. The defeat was devastating, but confession and cleansing turned it into victory. God restores what sin forfeits.

Name: Shiloh
Description: Where the tabernacle stood for over 300 years and the ark rested. Hannah prayed here for a son, and young Samuel heard God's voice in the night.
BiblicalSignificance: Shiloh was where Israel met God for generations - until corruption emptied it of glory. Places don't guarantee God's presence; hearts do.

Name: Gibeon
Description: The Hivite city that tricked Israel into a treaty, then was defended by Joshua when the sun stood still. Later Solomon worshipped here, and God appeared to him in a dream offering anything he asked.
BiblicalSignificance: Gibeon reminds us that even our mistakes become God's instruments - Israel's foolish treaty became the stage for the longest day in history.

Name: Gibeah
Description: King Saul's hometown and capital. It was also the scene of the horrific crime in Judges 19 that nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin.
BiblicalSignificance: Gibeah shows how far a people can fall - and that God still raises leaders from broken places. Saul's story began with such promise here.

Name: Mizpah
Description: The assembly place where Samuel called Israel to repentance, put away their idols, and watched God thunder against the Philistines. Samuel set up the Ebenezer stone here: 'Thus far the Lord has helped us.'
BiblicalSignificance: Mizpah is the geography of return - repentance, prayer, and a stone of remembrance. 'Thus far' looks back with gratitude and forward with hope.

Name: Ramah
Description: Samuel's hometown, where he judged Israel and where the elders demanded a king. Deborah held court between Ramah and Bethel.
BiblicalSignificance: Ramah witnessed Israel's fateful demand - 'give us a king' - trading God's direct rule for a human one. Even our rejections become part of His redemptive plan.

Name: Jerusalem
Description: David's capital, Solomon's temple city, the place of Jesus's death and resurrection, and the birthplace of the church at Pentecost. No city looms larger in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Jerusalem is where God's story concentrates - temple, cross, empty tomb, Spirit. What happened there anchors every hope we have.
RelatedPeople: King David; King Solomon; Jesus; Simon Peter
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; Building of Solomon's Temple; David Becomes King; Davidic Covenant; David and Bathsheba; The Kingdom Divides; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Ezra Reads the Law; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Triumphal Entry; The Last Supper; Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection; The Ascension; Pentecost; Jerusalem Council; Martyrdom of Stephen

Name: Mount Carmel
Description: The mountain overlooking the Mediterranean where Elijah faced 450 prophets of Baal in the great contest - fire from heaven deciding who is truly God.
BiblicalSignificance: Carmel is where God answered by fire and a nation briefly remembered. Elijah's prayer - 'answer me, Lord, so these people will know' - still models bold, God-glorifying prayer.

Name: Tyre
Description: The wealthy Phoenician port whose king Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple - and whose princess Jezebel married Ahab, bringing Baal worship into Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: Tyre embodies the double edge of the nations: partner in building God's house, then pipeline for idolatry. Jesus later praised the faith He found in Tyre's region above Israel's unbelief.
RelatedPeople: King Solomon; King Ahab; Jezebel; Jesus

Name: Samaria
Description: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, built by Omri. Its kings led the nation into idolatry until Assyria carried it away. Jesus later crossed its prejudices at Jacob's well.
BiblicalSignificance: Samaria fell because its kings forgot God - yet grace kept reaching there: Elisha's miracles, Philip's revival, and a Samaritan woman who became an evangelist.
RelatedPeople: King Ahab; Elijah; Elisha; Jesus; The Samaritan Woman; Philip

Name: Nineveh
Description: The great Assyrian capital - 'the great city' of 120,000 people - to which Jonah reluctantly preached. To his dismay, they repented, and God spared them.
BiblicalSignificance: Nineveh proves God's mercy has no borders. The prophet wanted judgment; God wanted repentance. His compassion for the lost rebukes every narrow heart.

Name: Babylon
Description: The glittering empire that destroyed Jerusalem and carried Judah into exile - and the city where Daniel served kings, his friends survived the furnace, and God's people learned to sing the Lord's song in a strange land.
BiblicalSignificance: Babylon is Scripture's symbol of worldly power opposed to God - yet God ruled there too, humbling Nebuchadnezzar and raising Daniel. No exile is beyond His reach.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; King Nebuchadnezzar; Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; Ezekiel
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Daniel in the Lions' Den; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Name: Susa
Description: The Persian winter capital where Esther became queen and risked her life to save the Jews from Haman's genocide - and where Nehemiah served as the king's cupbearer before rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.
BiblicalSignificance: Susa shows God positioning His people in palaces of power 'for such a time as this.' Providence, not coincidence, put Esther and Nehemiah where history needed them.

Name: River Chebar
Description: The canal in Babylonia where the exiles settled - and where Ezekiel, among the captives, saw the heavens opened and the glory of God in visions.
BiblicalSignificance: By the Chebar, God proved He was not confined to Jerusalem's temple. His glory travels with His people, even into exile.

Name: Bethlehem
Description: The 'little town' of Ruth and Boaz, birthplace of David, and - as Micah foretold - birthplace of Jesus. Shepherds heard the angels here; wise men brought gifts here.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethlehem is God's pattern of choosing the small and overlooked. The Savior of the world arrived not in Rome but in a village - hope rarely looks the way we expect.
RelatedPeople: Ruth; Boaz; King David; Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Ruth's Loyalty

Name: Nazareth
Description: The Galilean hill town where Jesus grew up - 'Can anything good come from Nazareth?' His neighbors knew Him as the carpenter's son and rejected Him.
BiblicalSignificance: Nazareth reminds us that God hides glory in obscurity. Thirty hidden years in a despised town preceded three years that changed the world.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary

Name: Capernaum
Description: The fishing town Jesus made His home base - 'His own town.' Peter's house was here; the synagogue where He taught stands in ruins still. More miracles happened here than anywhere else.
BiblicalSignificance: Capernaum received the most light - and Jesus warned it faced the greatest accountability. Privilege without repentance becomes judgment.

Name: Galilee
Description: The northern region - 'Galilee of the Gentiles' - where Jesus grew up, called His disciples, preached the Sermon on the Mount, and walked on water. After the resurrection He met them here again.
BiblicalSignificance: Galilee was the despised north, far from Jerusalem's power - exactly where Jesus chose to begin. God still starts His greatest works in overlooked places.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; Andrew; James, Son of Zebedee; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Jesus Calms the Storm; The Feeding of the Five Thousand; Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana

Name: Bethany
Description: The village home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus - Jesus's retreat two miles from Jerusalem. Here He raised Lazarus, was anointed for burial, and ascended from nearby.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethany was where Jesus was loved as a friend, not just followed as a teacher. Sitting at His feet, like Mary, is still the one necessary thing.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary of Bethany; Martha; Lazarus

Name: Golgotha
Description: 'The Place of the Skull' - the hill outside Jerusalem's walls where Jesus was crucified between two criminals, with a nearby tomb where He was buried and rose.
BiblicalSignificance: Golgotha is the anchor point of the Christian hope - the place where justice and mercy met, sin was paid for, and death was defeated. Everything this blog proclaims flows from this hill.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; John the Apostle; Joseph of Arimathea

Name: Antioch
Description: The Syrian metropolis where believers were first called 'Christians.' From here Paul and Barnabas were sent out, and the gospel crossed decisively into the Gentile world.
BiblicalSignificance: Antioch proves the church was always meant to go - not a Jerusalem sect but a world mission. The name 'Christian' was born where the gospel crossed cultures.

Name: Ephesus
Description: The great Asian port where Paul taught for over two years, 'so that all who lived in Asia heard the word.' Home of the Artemis temple, the silversmiths' riot, and the church that lost its first love.
BiblicalSignificance: Ephesus had sound doctrine and lost its heart - Jesus's warning to return to first love still speaks to every busy, correct, cooling church.

Name: Corinth
Description: The wealthy, immoral Greek port where Paul planted a church and wrote two of his most famous letters - on love, resurrection, and grace for a messy congregation.
BiblicalSignificance: Corinth shows that no church is too broken for God to love and no people too messed up to become saints. Grace met Corinth's chaos and made it holy.

Name: Philippi
Description: The Roman colony where Paul's European mission began - Lydia's conversion by the river, the jailer's midnight baptism after an earthquake, and the joyful letter Paul later wrote from prison.
BiblicalSignificance: Philippi is where the gospel first touched European soil - through a businesswoman, a slave girl, and a jailer. God builds His church from the most unlikely people.

Name: Thessalonica
Description: The Macedonian capital where Paul preached three Sabbaths, a church was born amid riots, and Paul wrote his earliest letters - full of teaching on Christ's return.
BiblicalSignificance: Thessalonica's young believers turned to God 'from idols' and waited eagerly for Jesus's return. New faith with old hope - the pattern for every generation.

Name: Colossae
Description: The small Lycus Valley town Paul never visited, yet loved enough to write one of his richest letters - exalting Christ's supremacy against every rival philosophy.
BiblicalSignificance: Colossae proves you don't have to be a major city to matter to God. A small church received one of the Bible's greatest declarations of who Jesus is.

Name: Patmos
Description: The small rocky island where the aged apostle John was exiled 'for the word of God' - and where he received the Revelation, the Bible's final book.
BiblicalSignificance: Patmos turns exile into vision. Banished and alone, John saw the throne, the Lamb, and the new heaven and earth. Our bleakest places can become our clearest views of Christ.

Name: Rome
Description: The empire's capital and Paul's long-desired destination. He arrived in chains, preached from house arrest for two years, wrote his greatest letter to its church, and was martyred here under Nero.
BiblicalSignificance: Rome is where the gospel marched into the heart of worldly power - in chains, yet 'unhindered.' Kingdoms rise and fall; the word of God cannot be chained.

Name: Abana
Description: One of the rivers of Damascus, named by Naaman who asked whether they were not better than all the waters of Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: Abana is the river Naaman preferred, until he washed in the Jordan.

Name: Abel-beth-maachah
Description: A northern border city, called a mother in Israel, where the wise woman saved the city from Joab by delivering Sheba's head.
BiblicalSignificance: Abel-beth-maachah is where one wise woman's words stopped Joab's siege and saved a city.

Name: Abel-meholah
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the Jordan Valley, Israel
Description: A Jordan Valley town, home of Elisha, near where Gideon's enemies fled toward Zererah.
BiblicalSignificance: Abel-meholah is Elisha's hometown, the plowman's village from which Elijah called him.

Name: Abilene
ModernLocation: Around Abila, northwest of Damascus, Syria
Description: A small tetrarchy ruled by Lysanias, named by Luke when dating the start of John the Baptist's ministry.
BiblicalSignificance: Abilene is one more fixed point in Luke's historical frame for the gospel story.

Name: Accad
Description: One of Nimrod's first cities in Shinar, and the name behind Akkad, the first great Mesopotamian empire. Its site is not stated in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Accad is a first-city name, kept as Scripture keeps it: named, and no more.

Name: Aceldama
ModernLocation: Jerusalem, in the Valley of Hinnom
Description: The field bought with Judas' blood money, called the field of blood, used to bury strangers.
BiblicalSignificance: Aceldama is the grim footnote to betrayal: thirty pieces of silver bought a burial ground, not a kingdom.

Name: Achaia
Description: The Roman province of southern Greece, including Athens and Corinth, where Paul preached a year and a half.
BiblicalSignificance: Achaia is where the gospel met Athens' philosophers and Corinth's crowds, and stayed to build churches.

Name: Admah
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southern Dead Sea region
Description: One of the cities of the plain, destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah.
BiblicalSignificance: Admah is named in the judgment lists as a city that perished with its neighbours.

Name: Adramyttium
Description: A port of Asia Minor whose ship carried Paul, a prisoner, from Caesarea toward Rome by the Asian coast.
BiblicalSignificance: Adramyttium lent its ship to Paul's first leg to Rome, coastwise toward Myra.

Name: Adria
ModernLocation: Adriatic Sea, between Italy and the Balkans
Description: The sea in which Paul's ship was driven up and down fourteen stormy nights before the wreck on Malta.
BiblicalSignificance: Adria is the storm sea of Acts 27, where Paul's promise held and every soul survived.

Name: Adullam
Description: A Canaanite royal city near which David hid in the cave of Adullam, gathering the distressed and discontented around him.
BiblicalSignificance: Adullam's cave is where David's mighty men first gathered: debtors and malcontents who became his army.

Name: Aenon
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally placed in the Jordan Valley near Salim
Description: A place of much water near Salim where John the Baptist was baptizing while Jesus' disciples also baptized.
BiblicalSignificance: Aenon marks the overlap of John's ministry and Jesus' rising ministry, just before John was imprisoned.

Name: Aijalon
Description: A Levitical city in Dan's territory, in the valley where Joshua commanded the sun to stand still and where Saul pursued the Philistines.
BiblicalSignificance: Aijalon's valley is where the sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon over Aijalon, in Israel's longest day.

Name: Alexandria
Description: Egypt's great port and learning center, home of Apollos the eloquent preacher and of the ship that carried Paul toward Rome.
BiblicalSignificance: Alexandria links the gospel's learning and its travel: eloquence for the churches, a ship for the prisoner.

Name: Almon-diblathaim
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. A camp in Moab on the final approach to the Jordan. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Alush
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ammon
Description: The kingdom east of the Jordan, descended from Lot's younger son. Ammon warred with Israel from the judges to the exile, and its capital Rabbah fell to David.
BiblicalSignificance: Ammon is a standing reminder that old hostilities run deep, and that God judges nations as surely as individuals.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 2:19; Judges 11:12; Jeremiah 49:1; Judges 11:4; 2 Samuel 11:1; 1 Kings 11:7

Name: Amphipolis
Description: A Macedonian city on the same road, through which Paul passed on the way to Thessalonica.
BiblicalSignificance: Amphipolis is another road city on Paul's way to Thessalonica's synagogue.

Name: Anathoth
Description: A Levitical town in Benjamin, home of Jeremiah and of Abiathar, where Jeremiah bought a field as a sign of return.
BiblicalSignificance: Anathoth is Jeremiah's hometown, whose men plotted against him, and where he bought land in a besieged city as hope of return.

Name: Antioch in Pisidia
Description: The inland city of Pisidia, distinct from Syrian Antioch, where Paul preached his great synagogue sermon and was driven out.
BiblicalSignificance: Antioch in Pisidia is where Paul's synagogue preaching turned to the Gentiles after Jewish rejection.

Name: Antipatris
Description: A town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, built by Herod and named for his father, where soldiers escorted Paul by night.
BiblicalSignificance: Antipatris is a night-stop on Paul's hurried journey from a Jerusalem plot to a Caesarean trial.

Name: Aphek
Description: A Philistine border town where the ark was captured in Eli's day and where the Philistines mustered before Gilboa.
BiblicalSignificance: Aphek is where Israel lost the ark and Eli's sons fell, and where the Philistine lords gathered against Saul.
RelatedPeople: Eli; Samuel; King Saul; King David

Name: Apollonia
Description: A Macedonian city on the road from Philippi to Thessalonica, through which Paul passed without stopping to preach.
BiblicalSignificance: Apollonia is a passed-through city on Paul's Macedonian road.

Name: Appii Forum
ModernLocation: Near Rome, Italy (on the Appian Way)
Description: A market town on the Appian Way where Roman brethren came out to meet Paul, and he thanked God and took courage.
BiblicalSignificance: Appii Forum is where Paul, prisoner no longer alone, met the church coming down the road to him.

Name: Ar
Description: A chief city of Moab on the Arnon, named in the wilderness journey and in Isaiah's oracle against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Ar is Moab's border city, named at the crossing and in the ruin.

Name: Arabah
ModernLocation: The Jordan Rift Valley from the Sea of Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba
Description: The long rift valley running south from the Dead Sea, crossed by Israel on the wilderness journey and marking the eastern edge of Judah.
BiblicalSignificance: The Arabah frames the final approach to the Promised Land and the setting of Moses' farewell speeches.

Name: Arabia
Description: The desert lands south and east of Israel, home of traders, kings bringing gifts to Solomon, and the peoples named in the oracles against the nations.
BiblicalSignificance: Arabia's caravans and kings point to a day when all nations bring their wealth to the King.

Name: Arad
Description: A Canaanite royal city of the Negev whose king attacked Israel and was later destroyed at Hormah.
BiblicalSignificance: Arad is the first Canaanite city to fight Israel, and the first to fall when Israel vowed to destroy it.

Name: Aram
Description: The land of the Arameans, north and east of Israel, with Damascus as its great city. Aram warred with David, allied and fought with Israel's kings for centuries, and is also called Syria in the King James Version. Called Syria in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Aram shows how a near neighbour can be enemy, ally, and instrument of God in turn, and how God's word runs even to Damascus.
KeyScriptures: 2 Samuel 8:5; 1 Kings 11:25; Isaiah 7:8; Matthew 4:24; Acts 15:23; Acts 15:41

Name: Areopagus
Description: The rocky hill in Athens where the city's council met, also called Mars' Hill, where Paul preached the unknown God.
BiblicalSignificance: The Areopagus is where the gospel met philosophy face to face, and some believed.

Name: Arimathaea
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with Ramathaim in Judea
Description: The hometown of Joseph, the wealthy disciple who asked Pilate for Jesus' body and laid it in his own new tomb.
BiblicalSignificance: Arimathaea gave the church the tomb: a rich man's grave, fulfilling prophecy, emptied on the third day.

Name: Armenia
Description: The highland land to which Sennacherib's murderers fled, and a kingdom summoned against Babylon in Jeremiah.
BiblicalSignificance: Armenia is the refuge beyond the mountains, where even a fleeing king's sons disappear from the story.

Name: Arnon
Description: The gorge river that was the border of Moab and of Sihon's Amorite kingdom, crossed by Israel on the way to Canaan.
BiblicalSignificance: The Arnon is the border Israel crossed into its inheritance.

Name: Aroer
Description: A city on the edge of the Arnon valley, named in the conquest and in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Aroer is the Arnon's edge city, named in conquest and in ruin.

Name: Arpad
Description: A Syrian city conquered by Assyria, named in the taunt against Jerusalem and in the oracle against Damascus.
BiblicalSignificance: Arpad is the fallen neighbour held up to frighten Jerusalem.

Name: Arvad
Description: The island city off the Syrian coast whose mariners and warriors manned Tyre's ships and walls.
BiblicalSignificance: Arvad is the island of sailors, serving the merchant city.

Name: Ashdod
Description: A Philistine royal city where the captured ark toppled Dagon, and a port city denounced by the prophets. Called Azotus in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Ashdod is where Dagon fell face down before the ark, and where the ark's presence broke the city's idol.

Name: Ashkelon
Description: A Philistine royal city on the coast, taken briefly by Judah, later a byword for Philistine pride under judgment.
BiblicalSignificance: Ashkelon is named in Samson's riddle-vengeance and in the prophets' oracles against Philistia.

Name: Ashteroth
Description: A royal city of Og king of Bashan, famed for its goddess, taken by Israel and given to Manasseh.
BiblicalSignificance: Ashteroth is Og's city, whose name kept the memory of the goddess even after Israel took it.

Name: Asia
Description: The wealthy Roman province of western Asia Minor, where Paul preached two years at Ephesus and all Asia heard the word.
BiblicalSignificance: Asia is where the gospel took a province: seven churches, two years, and a riot over silver shrines.

Name: Asshur
Description: The ancient Assyrian city of Assur, named in the Table of Nations as built by Asshur, and the city from which Assyria took its name.
BiblicalSignificance: Asshur is the city that gave an empire its name.

Name: Assos
Description: A coastal town of Asia Minor where Paul rejoined his companions on foot after Miletus.
BiblicalSignificance: Assos is a footnote of Paul's walking pace: he chose the road while the ship sailed around.

Name: Assyria
Description: The great Mesopotamian empire whose capital was Nineveh. Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel, deporting its people in 722 BC, and later threatened Judah under Sennacherib.
BiblicalSignificance: Assyria is the rod of God's anger in Isaiah, yet also the object of His mercy: the Ninevites repented at Jonah's preaching.

Name: Athens
Description: The famed city of philosophers, full of idols, where Paul reasoned in the synagogue and marketplace and preached on the Areopagus.
BiblicalSignificance: Athens is where the gospel met the world's wisdom, and a few, including Dionysius, believed.

Name: Attalia
Description: The Pamphylian port from which Paul and Barnabas sailed back to Syrian Antioch at the end of the first journey.
BiblicalSignificance: Attalia is the harbor home of the first journey's end.

Name: Ava
Description: A Mesopotamian city whose people were settled in Samaria. Its exact site is not stated, and it is distinct from the Gaza-area Avvim.
BiblicalSignificance: Ava is one of Samaria's resettled peoples, distinct from the Avvim of the coast.

Name: Azekah
Description: A Judahite fortress town in the Elah Valley, on the Philistine border, besieged by Nebuchadnezzar among Judah's last strongholds.
BiblicalSignificance: Azekah guarded the Elah Valley road, and its name appears in Jeremiah's account of Judah's final days.

Name: Baal-meon
Description: A Moabite city named in the conquest lists and in the oracles against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Baal-meon is a Moabite city named in conquest and in judgment alike.

Name: Baal-peor
Description: The Moabite cult place where Israel joined in Baal worship and was plagued, named in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Hosea, and the psalms.
BiblicalSignificance: Baal-peor is where Israel's worship went astray at the edge of the land.

Name: Bamoth-baal
Description: A Moabite high place where Balak took Balaam to curse Israel, named in Numbers and Joshua.
BiblicalSignificance: Bamoth-baal is a high place of cursing that became a place of blessing.

Name: Bashan
ModernLocation: Transjordan plateau northeast of Gilead, modern Syria-Jordan border region
Description: The fertile plateau kingdom of Og, conquered by Israel under Moses and given to half of Manasseh.
BiblicalSignificance: Bashan's conquest showed Israel that even giant kings could not stand against God, and its oaks and bulls became proverbial for strength.

Name: Beautiful Gate
Description: A gate of the temple called Beautiful, where a lame man begged daily until Peter and John healed him in Jesus' name.
BiblicalSignificance: The Beautiful Gate is where the first apostolic miracle turned a beggar into a leaper and a crowd into witnesses.

Name: Beer-elim
Description: A Moabite well-town named in Isaiah's oracle against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Beer-elim is a well-town named once, in Moab's ruin.

Name: Beer Lahai Roi
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the Negev between Kadesh and Bered
Description: The well where the angel of the Lord found Hagar, named "the well of him that liveth and seeth me," later Isaac's dwelling place.
BiblicalSignificance: Beer Lahai Roi is where God saw Hagar in her affliction, the first well named for God seeing the unseen.

Name: Beeroth
Description: One of the four Gibeonite cities that made peace with Joshua by cunning, later a Benjamite town.
BiblicalSignificance: Beeroth is one of the cities whose treaty trick bound Israel to an oath, and whose men later murdered Ish-bosheth.

Name: Bene-jaakan
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Berea
Description: A Macedonian city whose Jews searched the Scriptures daily to test Paul's preaching, and were called more noble than Thessalonica's.
BiblicalSignificance: Berea is the model of the Berean habit: receive the word eagerly, and check it daily.

Name: Berothai
Description: A city of Hadadezer from which David took much brass. Its parallel name in Chronicles is Cun.
BiblicalSignificance: Berothai gave its brass to the house of God.

Name: Beth-peor
Description: The valley in Moab opposite Beth-peor where Moses died and was buried by God, and where Israel camped before the law's second giving.
BiblicalSignificance: Beth-peor is the valley of Moses' grave, known to God alone.

Name: Beth-shemesh
Description: A Levitical border town between Judah and Philistia, to which the ark returned on a cart drawn by milk cows.
BiblicalSignificance: Beth-shemesh is where the ark came home, and where its people learned that even curiosity about holy things has a cost.

Name: Bethphage
ModernLocation: On the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem
Description: A village on the Mount of Olives where Jesus sent disciples to fetch the colt for His entry into Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethphage is the staging point of the Triumphal Entry, where Jesus openly claimed His kingship.

Name: Bethsaida
ModernLocation: El-Araj or et-Tell, northern shore of the Sea of Galilee (debated)
Description: A fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, home of Philip, Andrew, and Peter, where Jesus healed a blind man and fed the five thousand nearby.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethsaida heard much of Jesus' teaching and saw His miracles, yet He pronounced woe on it for unbelief.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Name: Bethshan
Description: A strong Canaanite city on the Jezreel road where the Philistines hung the bodies of Saul and his sons on the wall.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethshan's wall is where Saul's body hung until the men of Jabesh-gilead came by night to bury him.

Name: Bezer
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the Transjordan wilderness, Jordan
Description: A city of refuge in Reuben's territory, in the wilderness of the plateau, appointed by Moses.
BiblicalSignificance: Bezer is one of the three refuge cities Moses set apart east of the Jordan.

Name: Bithynia
ModernLocation: Northern Turkey along the Black Sea
Description: A province on the Black Sea coast which Paul tried to enter, but the Spirit would not allow him.
BiblicalSignificance: Bithynia is where the Spirit said no, redirecting the gospel from Asia toward Europe.

Name: Bozrah
Description: The fortified capital region of Edom, denounced by the prophets as the city of the winepress of God's judgment.
BiblicalSignificance: Bozrah is Edom's stronghold, named in Isaiah's vision of the Lord coming with garments stained red.

Name: Brook Besor
Description: The brook in the Negev where two hundred of David's exhausted men stayed behind while the rest pursued the Amalekites.
BiblicalSignificance: Besor is where David made the law that the spoil belongs equally to those who fight and those who stay with the baggage.

Name: Brook Cherith
ModernLocation: Unknown; east of the Jordan, Jordan
Description: The brook east of the Jordan where Elijah hid during the drought and was fed by ravens.
BiblicalSignificance: Cherith is the hidden brook of the drought, where ravens brought bread to the prophet.

Name: Brook Kidron
ModernLocation: Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, Israel
Description: The brook valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, crossed by David fleeing Absalom and by the temple reforms' debris.
BiblicalSignificance: Kidron is the valley of tears David crossed barefoot, and the ditch where idolatry was burned.

Name: Brook Kishon
Description: The seasonal stream of the Jezreel Valley that swept away Sisera's army and beside which Elijah slew Baal's prophets.
BiblicalSignificance: Kishon is the ancient river that swept the Canaanite host away, and where Baal's prophets fell.

Name: Caesarea Philippi
Description: A city at the foot of Mount Hermon, renamed for Philip the tetrarch and Caesar, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ.
BiblicalSignificance: Caesarea Philippi is where the church's confession was born: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.'

Name: Caesarea
ModernLocation: Caesarea Maritima, on the Mediterranean coast of Israel
Description: Herod's great port city, capital of Roman Judea, where Cornelius was converted, Philip lived, and Paul was imprisoned two years.
BiblicalSignificance: Caesarea is where the gospel first entered a Gentile home, and where Paul waited for his appeal to Caesar.
RelatedEvents: Peter and Cornelius; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Name: Calah
Description: A great city of Assyria named in the Table of Nations, later the Assyrian royal city of Calah, modern Nimrud.
BiblicalSignificance: Calah is Assyria's ancient root, named before Assyria was an empire.

Name: Calneh
Description: One of Nimrod's first cities in Shinar, later named by Amos among the great cities that fell.
BiblicalSignificance: Calneh, great in Nimrod's day and a warning in Amos's, shows that great cities fall.

Name: Cana
ModernLocation: Kafr Kanna or Khirbet Qana, Galilee (debated)
Description: A village in Galilee where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, His first sign.
BiblicalSignificance: Cana is where Jesus' glory was first revealed, and where His disciples first believed.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana

Name: Caphtor
Description: The homeland from which the Philistines came, named in Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Amos. Traditionally identified with Crete.
BiblicalSignificance: Caphtor reminds us that even Israel's fiercest neighbours had an origin and a history God knew.

Name: Cappadocia
Description: The high plateau province of central Asia Minor, whose people were at Pentecost and to whom Peter later wrote.
BiblicalSignificance: Cappadocia heard the gospel at Pentecost and received it again in Peter's letter.

Name: Carchemish
Description: The Euphrates fortress city where Pharaoh Necho was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar in 605 BC, the battle that made Babylon master of the Near East and set the course of Judah's exile.
BiblicalSignificance: Carchemish is the hinge of empires: Egypt fell there, and Judah's fate was sealed.

Name: Carmel
Description: A Judahite town in the hill country, home of Nabal, whose wife Abigail saved his house from David.
BiblicalSignificance: Carmel is Nabal's town, where Abigail's wisdom turned David from bloodguilt.

Name: Cenchrea
Description: Corinth's eastern port, home of a church whose deaconess Phoebe carried Paul's letter to Rome.
BiblicalSignificance: Cenchrea gave Rome its letter-bearer: Phoebe, servant of its church, carried Romans.

Name: Chaldea
Description: The land of the Chaldeans, the ruling people of Neo-Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar. Its armies destroyed Jerusalem, and its learning and astrology framed Daniel's exile.
BiblicalSignificance: Chaldea is the power God used to chasten Judah, and the power whose pride He then brought down.

Name: Chios
Description: An Aegean island past which Paul's ship sailed on the voyage from Troas to Miletus.
BiblicalSignificance: Chios is a landmark on Paul's Aegean crossing, named in a single sailing note.

Name: Chittim
Description: The "isles of Chittim" named among Javan's sons, and later the ships of Chittim that come against kings in Daniel. Traditionally identified with Cyprus and the western isles.
BiblicalSignificance: Chittim marks the western horizon of the biblical world, the isles beyond the sea.

Name: Chorazin
Description: A Galilean town near Capernaum where Jesus performed many mighty works.
BiblicalSignificance: Chorazin stands as a warning: privilege without repentance brings a heavier judgment.

Name: Cilicia
Description: The coastal province of Paul's birth city Tarsus, through which he traveled confirming the churches.
BiblicalSignificance: Cilicia is Paul's home province, and the road he walked to strengthen what he had planted.

Name: Clauda
Description: A small island south of Crete under which Paul's ship ran for shelter and barely secured the lifeboat.
BiblicalSignificance: Clauda is where the storm's grip tightened and the crew fought to save the boat itself.

Name: Cnidus
Description: A headland city of Asia Minor which Paul's ship reached with difficulty against the wind.
BiblicalSignificance: Cnidus is where the wind first fought Paul's voyage, and the storm began to win.

Name: Coos
Description: An Aegean island, spelled Coos in the KJV, where Paul's ship came on the voyage from Miletus to Rhodes.
BiblicalSignificance: Coos is a sailing note on Paul's final free voyage, island by island toward Jerusalem.

Name: Crete
Description: The large island south of Greece, whose people were at Pentecost, where Paul was shipwrecked off course and where Titus was left to set things in order.
BiblicalSignificance: Crete is where Paul's voyage nearly ended, and where Titus was left to appoint elders.

Name: Cuthah
Description: A Mesopotamian city whose people were settled in Samaria after Israel's deportation, and from whom the Samaritans were later called Cuthites by tradition.
BiblicalSignificance: Cuthah is the city whose settlers became Samaria's new people.

Name: Cyprus
Description: The great island of the eastern Mediterranean, Barnabas' homeland, where Paul and Barnabas preached on the first missionary journey.
BiblicalSignificance: Cyprus is where the first missionary journey began, and where a proconsul believed.

Name: Cyrene
Description: The great Greek city of North Africa, home of Simon who carried Jesus' cross, and of men who preached to Greeks at Antioch.
BiblicalSignificance: Cyrene gave the cross a bearer and Antioch some of its first Greek preachers.

Name: Dalmanutha
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the western shore of the Sea of Galilee near Magdala
Description: A place on the Sea of Galilee's western shore, named only in Mark, where Jesus landed after feeding the four thousand and was met by Pharisees demanding a sign.
BiblicalSignificance: Dalmanutha is where Jesus refused to perform on demand, and left again by boat.

Name: Dalmatia
Description: The Adriatic coast province where Titus went when Paul, near the end, was left almost alone.
BiblicalSignificance: Dalmatia is where Titus carried the work on while Paul waited in a Roman prison.

Name: Damascus
Description: The great city of Aram, the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world. David garrisoned it, its kings warred with Israel for generations, and on its road Saul the persecutor met the risen Christ in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Damascus is where enemies become apostles: the road to Damascus runs through both testaments.

Name: Dan
Description: The northernmost city of Israel, settled by the tribe of Dan after they took Laish and renamed it, marking the proverbial border "from Dan to Beersheba."
BiblicalSignificance: Dan marks Israel's northern edge, and also its idolatry: Jeroboam set up a golden calf here.

Name: Dead Sea
Description: The salt sea at the lowest place on earth, also called the Salt Sea, bordering the cities of the plain and the wilderness of Judah.
BiblicalSignificance: The Dead Sea is the sea of judgment over the plain, and the border of the promised land's eastern side.

Name: Debir
Description: A Canaanite royal city, also called Kirjath-sepher, taken by Othniel, who won Caleb's daughter Achsah for it.
BiblicalSignificance: Debir is the city of the book, taken by Othniel for love of Achsah, and a Levitical city in Judah.

Name: Decapolis
ModernLocation: East of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, Jordan/Syria
Description: A league of ten largely Gentile cities east of Galilee, where Jesus healed the demoniac and the deaf man.
BiblicalSignificance: The Decapolis shows Jesus' ministry reaching beyond Jewish territory, and its people spread His fame abroad.

Name: Dedan
Description: An Arabian trading people and place, named in the oracles against Edom and among the merchants of Tyre.
BiblicalSignificance: Dedan stands at the crossroads of the desert trade, and under the same judgment as its neighbours.

Name: Derbe
Description: A frontier town of Lycaonia where Paul and Barnabas preached and made many disciples before turning back.
BiblicalSignificance: Derbe is the turnaround point of the first journey, where the missionaries doubled back to strengthen new churches.

Name: Dibon-gad
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. A camp near Dibon on the final approach to the Jordan. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Dibon
Description: A Moabite city rebuilt by Gad, later famous for the Mesha Stele, the Moabite Stone, found there.
BiblicalSignificance: Dibon is where Mesha king of Moab recorded his revolt against Israel, a stone that still speaks.

Name: Dimon
Description: A Moabite town or stream named in Isaiah's oracle, whose waters would be full of blood.
BiblicalSignificance: Dimon is the waters of blood in Moab's oracle.

Name: Dophkah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Dothan
Description: A town on the road to Egypt where Joseph's brothers sold him, and where Elisha's servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire.
BiblicalSignificance: Dothan is where Joseph was cast into a pit and where Elisha opened blind eyes to an army of fire.

Name: Dumah
Description: A place named in Isaiah's oracle, "the burden of Dumah," where a watchman is asked what of the night. Its exact location is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Dumah is a night-watch oracle: a question asked in darkness, answered with the coming morning.

Name: Dura
Description: The plain in Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden image, and where Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow and walked from the furnace unharmed.
BiblicalSignificance: Dura is the plain of the golden image, and of the fourth Man in the fire.

Name: Ebronah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ecbatana
Description: Called Achmetha in Ezra, the Median capital where the scroll of Cyrus's decree was found, authorising the rebuilding of the temple.
BiblicalSignificance: Ecbatana is where a lost decree was found, and the rebuilding went on.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Name: Eden
Description: A Mesopotamian trading place named with Haran and Canneh among Tyre's merchants, and as a conquered people in the Assyrian boast. It is distinct from the Garden of Eden.
BiblicalSignificance: This Eden is a market town, not a paradise: a reminder that Scripture reuses names and the context must decide.

Name: Edom
ModernLocation: Southern Jordan and northern Saudi Arabia
Description: The land of Esau's descendants, also called Seir, south-east of the Dead Sea. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness, rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall, and is judged by Obadiah and others.
BiblicalSignificance: Edom warns that brotherhood spurned turns to bitterness, and that God sees how nations treat His people.

Name: Edrei
Description: A royal city of Og king of Bashan, where Israel defeated him in battle before taking the land.
BiblicalSignificance: Edrei is where Og's last stand fell, and Bashan passed to Israel.

Name: Eglaim
Description: A Moabite town named in Isaiah's oracle, where the cry of Moab's ruin is heard.
BiblicalSignificance: Eglaim is a cry-town in Moab's lament.

Name: Eglon
Description: A Canaanite royal city whose king joined the alliance against Gibeon and was hanged by Joshua at Makkedah.
BiblicalSignificance: Eglon is one of the five Amorite kings defeated at Gibeon, whose defeat opened the south to Israel.

Name: Ekron
Description: The northernmost Philistine royal city, where the ark rested on its way home and whose god Baal-zebub Ahaziah consulted.
BiblicalSignificance: Ekron is where the ark paused on its journey home, and whose god gave the New Testament its name for the devil's prince.

Name: Elam
Description: An ancient kingdom east of Babylon, with its capital at Susa. Elamites were among the peoples settled in Samaria, Elam is judged in Jeremiah, and Daniel saw his vision of the ram and the goat by the river Ulai in Elam.
BiblicalSignificance: Elam stands among the nations God judges and yet names among those who will one day be gathered.

Name: Elath
Description: The Red Sea port at the head of the gulf, paired with Ezion-geber, held by Judah, lost to Edom, and named in the kings' history.
BiblicalSignificance: Elath is the southern port, held and lost with the fortunes of Judah.

Name: Elealeh
Description: A Moabite city named in the conquest lists and in the oracles, whose vineyards and shouting are lamented in Isaiah.
BiblicalSignificance: Elealeh is Moab's vineyard city, lamented in the oracle.

Name: Elim
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The oasis of twelve wells and seventy palm trees where Israel camped after Marah. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ellasar
Description: The kingdom of Arioch, one of the four kings who warred against the cities of the plain and were defeated by Abram.
BiblicalSignificance: Ellasar is one of the four kings' lands, beaten by Abram's household army.

Name: Emmaus
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with Emmaus-Nicopolis or Qubeibeh (debated)
Description: A village about sixty furlongs from Jerusalem, where the risen Jesus walked with two disciples and broke bread with them.
BiblicalSignificance: Emmaus is where downcast disciples learned to see the whole Scripture pointing to Christ.

Name: En Gedi
ModernLocation: Ein Gedi, western Dead Sea shore, Israel
Description: An oasis town above the Dead Sea where David cut Saul's robe in a cave and spared his life.
BiblicalSignificance: En Gedi is the desert spring where David proved his innocence, cutting a robe instead of a throat.

Name: Endor
Description: A town in Manasseh where Saul, on the eve of Gilboa, consulted a medium to call up Samuel.
BiblicalSignificance: Endor is where Saul, abandoned by prophets and dreams, sought a forbidden voice and heard his doom.

Name: Erech
Description: One of Nimrod's first cities in the land of Shinar, named at the head of his kingdom list.
BiblicalSignificance: Erech is among the first cities Scripture names, raised by the first empire-builder.

Name: Eshtaol
Description: A Danite town near Zorah, where the Spirit of the Lord began to move Samson.
BiblicalSignificance: Eshtaol is where Samson's story stirs: the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Name: Etham
ModernLocation: Unknown; on the edge of the wilderness, Egypt
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ethiopia
Description: The African kingdom south of Egypt, called Cush in the genealogies. It appears in prophecies of judgment and of distant peoples coming to know God, and its borders marked the edge of the Persian empire.
BiblicalSignificance: Ethiopia reminds us that God's purposes reach to the ends of the earth, beyond every familiar border.

Name: Euphrates
Description: The great river of Mesopotamia, one of the four rivers of Eden and the promised eastern boundary of Israel's land, crossed by patriarchs, armies, and prophets.
BiblicalSignificance: The Euphrates is the boundary river of promise, from Eden to Revelation.

Name: Ezion-gaber
ModernLocation: Unknown; at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The Red Sea port on the journey's edge, later Solomon's fleet harbour. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ezion-geber
Description: The Red Sea port where Solomon built ships for the voyage to Ophir, at the edge of Edom.
BiblicalSignificance: Ezion-geber is Solomon's navy yard, the port of the gold ships.

Name: Fair Havens
Description: A small harbor on Crete's south coast where Paul's ship wintered in debate, and where Paul warned against sailing on.
BiblicalSignificance: Fair Havens is where Paul's warning was overruled, and the voyage pressed on into disaster.

Name: Gabbatha
Description: The stone pavement in Jerusalem where Pilate sat in judgment over Jesus; in Hebrew called Gabbatha.
BiblicalSignificance: Gabbatha is where the world's judge was judged by a Roman governor, and the crowd chose Barabbas.

Name: Gadara
Description: The city behind the KJV's 'country of the Gadarenes' (Mark, Luke) and 'country of the Gergesenes' (Matthew), where Jesus cast out the legion of demons.
BiblicalSignificance: Gadara is where Gentile territory first saw Jesus' power over the demonic, and the healed man became its first witness.

Name: Galatia
Description: The province of central Asia Minor where Paul founded churches and to which he wrote his fiercest letter about grace.
BiblicalSignificance: Galatia is where Paul fought for the gospel itself: not by works of the law, but by faith in Christ.

Name: Gath
Description: A Philistine royal city, home of Goliath, where David twice took refuge with Achish.
BiblicalSignificance: Gath is Goliath's city and David's unlikely refuge, where he feigned madness before its king.

Name: Gaza
Description: A Philistine royal city on the coastal road to Egypt, where Samson carried off the city gates and later died pulling down Dagon's temple.
BiblicalSignificance: Gaza is Samson's city of triumph and death, and the southern gate of Canaan on the way to Egypt.

Name: Gebal
Description: The ancient Phoenician port, called Byblos by the Greeks, whose skilled caulkers worked on Tyre's ships and whose land belonged to the unconquered coast.
BiblicalSignificance: Gebal is the old port whose craftsmen served the ships of Tyre.

Name: Gerar
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the western Negev, Israel
Description: A Philistine-region city of Abimelech, where Abraham and later Isaac sojourned and dug wells.
BiblicalSignificance: Gerar is where God protected Sarah and Rebekah, and where Isaac's wells became a covenant of peace.

Name: Gethsemane
ModernLocation: Foot of the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem
Description: The olive grove across the Kidron where Jesus prayed in agony on the night of His betrayal.
BiblicalSignificance: Gethsemane is where Jesus submitted to the Father's will, sweating as it were great drops of blood.

Name: Gezer
Description: A strategic Canaanite city on the road from the coast to Jerusalem, given to Solomon by Pharaoh as a wedding gift and rebuilt by him.
BiblicalSignificance: Gezer guarded the approach to Jerusalem and became a Solomonic fortress city with its famous gate.

Name: Gihon
Description: The second river of Eden, compassing the land of Ethiopia. It is distinct from the Gihon spring at Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Gihon of Eden must not be confused with Jerusalem's spring: Scripture names both.

Name: Gilead
ModernLocation: Transjordan highlands east of the Jordan, modern Jordan
Description: The mountainous region east of the Jordan settled by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, named for the heap of stones Jacob and Laban raised.
BiblicalSignificance: Gilead is the land of Jacob's covenant with Laban, of Jephthah and the Gileadite warriors, and of Elijah the Tishbite.

Name: Golan
ModernLocation: Unknown; in Bashan, Jordan-Syria border region
Description: A city of refuge in Manasseh's Bashan territory, appointed by Moses.
BiblicalSignificance: Golan is one of the three refuge cities Moses set apart east of the Jordan.

Name: Gomorrah
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southern Dead Sea region
Description: A city of the plain destroyed with Sodom in the overthrow of the cities of the plain. Called Gomorrha in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Gomorrah is named with Sodom ever after as the measure of a city ripe for judgment.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 19:24; Deuteronomy 29:23; Amos 4:11; Matthew 10:15; Mark 6:11; Romans 9:29
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Deuteronomy; Amos; Matthew; Mark; Romans

Name: Gozan
Description: The river and region in Assyria to which Israel was deported, on the river Habor.
BiblicalSignificance: Gozan is the exile's river country, where the ten tribes were carried.

Name: Great Sea
Description: The western sea, the Mediterranean, named as the western border of the promised land and in Ezekiel's vision of the temple stream.
BiblicalSignificance: The Great Sea is the western border, where the land ends and the isles begin.

Name: Habor
Description: The river of Gozan in Assyria, beside which deported Israel was settled.
BiblicalSignificance: Habor is the exile's river, named with Gozan and Halah.

Name: Halah
Description: An Assyrian place of exile for deported Israel, named with Habor and Gozan. Its exact site is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Halah is one of the exile's named places, kept unlocated.

Name: Hamath
Description: The great Syrian city on the Orontes, northern boundary of the promised land. Its king Toi congratulated David, and its name became a byword for a fallen great city in the prophets.
BiblicalSignificance: Hamath, the northern boundary stone, fell like the rest when Assyria came.

Name: Haradah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Hashmonah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Havilah
Description: A gold-bearing land named in the description of Eden's rivers and again in the Table of Nations and Ishmael's territory.
BiblicalSignificance: Havilah, rich in gold yet unlocated, reminds us how much of the earliest world Scripture sketches rather than maps.

Name: Hazarmaveth
Description: A Joktanite land in southern Arabia, traditionally the Hadramaut region of Yemen.
BiblicalSignificance: Hazarmaveth is one of the far Arabian names that fill out the Table of Nations to the south.

Name: Hazeroth
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The camp where Miriam was struck with leprosy for speaking against Moses. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Hazor
Description: The great Canaanite city of the north, head of the northern coalition Joshua defeated, later rebuilt and fortified by Solomon.
BiblicalSignificance: Hazor was the mightiest city Joshua burned, and the city whose king Jabin oppressed Israel until Deborah and Barak defeated him.

Name: Helam
Description: An Aramean place east of the Jordan where David defeated Hadadezer's army.
BiblicalSignificance: Helam is where David's victory over Aram was completed.

Name: Helbon
Description: A Syrian wine land named among the merchants of Tyre, famed for its wine.
BiblicalSignificance: Helbon is remembered for its wine, traded to the merchant city.

Name: Hena
Description: A city named in the Assyrian taunt beside Hamath and Arpad, whose gods did not deliver it. Its site is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Hena is a taunt-city, named to frighten Jerusalem and then forgotten.

Name: Heshbon
Description: The Amorite royal city of Sihon, taken by Israel and given to Reuben, later a Moabite city lamented by the prophets.
BiblicalSignificance: Heshbon is Sihon's capital, whose fall opened Transjordan to Israel, and whose ruins Isaiah mourns.

Name: Hiddekel
Description: The third river of Eden, the Tigris, named again as the great river beside which Daniel saw his vision of the linen-clad man.
BiblicalSignificance: Hiddekel, the Tigris by its Hebrew name, runs from Eden to Daniel's vision.

Name: Hierapolis
Description: A spa city near Laodicea and Colossae, whose church Epaphras labored for with great zeal.
BiblicalSignificance: Hierapolis is a church known only by a man's zeal for it, and by Paul's greeting.

Name: Hobah
Description: The place north of Damascus to which Abram pursued the kings who had taken Lot, as far as Hobah.
BiblicalSignificance: Hobah is the far point of Abram's night pursuit to rescue Lot.

Name: Hor-hagidgad
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Hormah
Description: The place in the Negev where Israel, after the spies' failure, was beaten back, and later destroyed the Canaanites in fulfillment of a vow.
BiblicalSignificance: Hormah is the place of both defeat and vow: Israel's presumption failed there, and its later obedience destroyed the cities.

Name: Horonaim
Description: A Moabite town named in Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles, on the road of flight from Moab's ruin.
BiblicalSignificance: Horonaim is the road of Moab's fugitives, named in lament.

Name: Iconium
Description: A leading city of Lycaonia where Paul and Barnabas preached boldly, performed signs, and fled a plot to stone them.
BiblicalSignificance: Iconium shows the pattern of Acts: bold speech, signs, division, and a narrow escape.

Name: Idumaea
ModernLocation: Southern Judea and the northern Negev
Description: The Greek name for Edom, south of Judea; crowds from Idumaea came to hear Jesus.
BiblicalSignificance: Idumaea shows how far Jesus' fame spread beyond Israel's old borders, drawing even Edom's descendants to Him.

Name: Ije-abarim
ModernLocation: Unknown; on the border of Moab, Jordan
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The ruins of Abarim on Moab's border, where Israel camped approaching the promised land. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Illyricum
Description: The province on the Adriatic's eastern shore, the far edge of Paul's preaching from Jerusalem round about.
BiblicalSignificance: Illyricum marks how far Paul's gospel had run by the time he wrote to Rome.

Name: Italy
Description: The Roman homeland, where Aquila and Priscilla had lived, where Paul landed at Puteoli, and where the church at Rome waited for him.
BiblicalSignificance: Italy is where Paul's appeal ended: the gospel reached the empire's heart.

Name: Ituraea
ModernLocation: Lebanon-Syria border region, north of Galilee
Description: A small tetrarchy northeast of Galilee, ruled by Philip the tetrarch when John the Baptist began preaching.
BiblicalSignificance: Ituraea dates the start of John's ministry, anchoring the gospel story in real rulers and real places.

Name: Ivah
Description: A city named in the Assyrian taunt beside Hamath and Arpad. Its site is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Ivah is a taunt-city, named to frighten Jerusalem and then forgotten.

Name: Jabbok
Description: The Transjordan river Jacob crossed on his return to Canaan, where he wrestled through the night and was renamed Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: The Jabbok is the river of wrestling, where Jacob became Israel.

Name: Jabesh-gilead
Description: A Gileadite town that failed to answer the muster against Benjamin, was rescued from Nahash by Saul, and whose men buried Saul and his sons.
BiblicalSignificance: Jabesh-gilead is the town Saul saved first and the town that buried him last.

Name: Jacob's Well
Description: The ancient well Jacob gave to Joseph, where Jesus asked a Samaritan woman for a drink and offered living water.
BiblicalSignificance: Jacob's Well is where Jesus revealed Himself as Messiah to an outcast and promised water that never runs dry.

Name: Jahaz
Description: The Moabite battleground where Sihon's army fell to Israel, named in the conquest story and in the oracles against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Jahaz is where Sihon's power broke, and Israel took the land.

Name: Jarmuth
Description: A Canaanite royal city whose king joined the alliance against Gibeon and fell at Makkedah.
BiblicalSignificance: Jarmuth is one of the five cities whose kings rose against Gibeon and fell to Joshua.

Name: Javan
Description: The Greek world, named among Japheth's sons and later among the nations trading with Tyre and hearing of God's glory.
BiblicalSignificance: Javan is the western world entering the biblical story, long before the gospel reached Greece.

Name: Jazer
Description: An Amorite town in Gilead taken by Israel, given to Gad, famed for its vineyards.
BiblicalSignificance: Jazer is the vineyard town of Gilead, taken by Moses' spies and settled by Gad.

Name: Jezreel
Description: An Israelite royal city with a palace of Ahab, beside Naboth's vineyard, where Jehu's purge began.
BiblicalSignificance: Jezreel is where Naboth was murdered for his vineyard and where Jehu judged the house of Ahab.

Name: Joppa
Description: The ancient seaport where Jonah boarded for Tarshish, and where Peter raised Dorcas and received the vision of the clean and unclean.
BiblicalSignificance: Joppa is where the door to the Gentiles swung open: Peter's rooftop vision sent him to Cornelius.
RelatedEvents: Peter and Cornelius; Jonah and Nineveh

Name: Jotbathah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. A land of rivers of waters, noted in Deuteronomy's retelling of the journey. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Judaea
Description: The Roman province covering southern Israel, home of Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and the temple; the KJV spelling of Judea.
BiblicalSignificance: Judaea is where Jesus was born, where He taught and was crucified, and where the church was born at Pentecost.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Name: Kedar
Description: A nomadic Arabian land named for Ishmael's son, known for its flocks, tents of black goat hair, and archers. Isaiah foretells the fall of Kedar's glory within a year.
BiblicalSignificance: Kedar stands for the desert peoples who live beyond the reach of cities, yet within the reach of prophecy.

Name: Kedesh
Description: A city of refuge in Naphtali, home of Barak, where Deborah sent for him to gather the tribes against Sisera.
BiblicalSignificance: Kedesh is the refuge city that sent Barak to battle, and the town of the judge who freed Israel.

Name: Kehelathah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Keilah
Description: A Judahite town David rescued from the Philistines, then fled when Saul pursued him and its people would have betrayed him.
BiblicalSignificance: Keilah is where David learned that gratitude is no guarantee: he saved the city, and it would have handed him to Saul.

Name: Kibroth-hattaavah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The graves of craving, where those who lusted for meat were buried. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Kir-hareseth
Description: A chief city of Moab, also called Kir-haresh and Kirheres, besieged by Israel and Judah in 2 Kings 3 and lamented in Isaiah and Jeremiah.
BiblicalSignificance: Kir-hareseth is Moab's fortress city, besieged and lamented.

Name: Kir
Description: The place to which Assyria deported the Arameans of Damascus, and a land named in the oracles of Isaiah and Amos. Its location is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Kir is the far end of exile for a conquered people, named and then left unmapped.

Name: Kiriath-jearim
Description: A Gibeonite city where the ark rested for twenty years in the house of Abinadab before David brought it to Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Kiriath-jearim kept the ark through the long silence between Eli and David, until David came to fetch it with dancing.

Name: Kiriathaim
Description: A Moabite city named in the war of the four kings, in the conquest lists, and in the oracles against Moab.
BiblicalSignificance: Kiriathaim is the ancient city of the Emim, named from Abram's day to Jeremiah's.

Name: Kirjath-huzoth
Description: A Moabite city where Balak brought Balaam and offered sacrifices before the cursing was attempted.
BiblicalSignificance: Kirjath-huzoth is the city of sacrifices before the blessing that could not be bought.

Name: Lachish
Description: A great fortified city of Judah, taken by Joshua, besieged by Sennacherib, and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar.
BiblicalSignificance: Lachish is the fortress whose siege Sennacherib carved on his palace walls, and whose letters cried for help as Judah fell.

Name: Land of Nod
Description: The land east of Eden to which Cain went after murdering Abel, where he built a city and his line began.
BiblicalSignificance: Nod is the land of wandering: the first exile, carrying the mark of Cain and the beginning of city-building apart from God.

Name: Land of Uz
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally northern Arabia or Edom
Description: The homeland of Job, named in his story and in the oracles against the nations. Its exact location is not stated in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Uz is where the question of suffering is asked most honestly, and where God answers out of the whirlwind.

Name: Laodicea
Description: A wealthy banking city of Asia, addressed in Revelation as lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, and urged to buy gold refined by fire.
BiblicalSignificance: Laodicea is the self-sufficient church, warned that wealth without Christ is wretchedness.

Name: Lasea
Description: A small Cretan city near Fair Havens, named once as the landmark of Paul's winter harbor.
BiblicalSignificance: Lasea is the near neighbor of Fair Havens, fixing the harbor on Crete's southern shore.

Name: Lebanon
Description: The mountain land north of Israel, famed for its cedars. Its timber built Solomon's temple and palace, and its heights are a byword for majesty in the prophets and the Song.
BiblicalSignificance: Lebanon's cedars became God's house, a picture of glory cut down and raised for His dwelling.

Name: Libnah
Description: A Levitical city of Judah that revolted from Jehoram, besieged by Sennacherib after Lachish. The same name also belongs to a station on the wilderness journey (Numbers 33:20), a distinct place sharing the name.
BiblicalSignificance: Libnah is the city that broke from Judah's apostate king, and the next stop on Sennacherib's campaign after Lachish.

Name: Libya
Description: The North African land west of Egypt, called Lubim in Nahum and Chronicles. Libyans marched with Egypt and with Gog, and are named among the nations judged.
BiblicalSignificance: Libya marks the western edge of Egypt's world, and one more nation in the reach of judgment.

Name: Lod
Description: A Benjamite town rebuilt by returned exiles, on the road between Joppa and Jerusalem. Called Lydda in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Lod is one of the towns the exiles rebuilt, a waypoint on the road from the coast to Jerusalem.

Name: Luhith
Description: A Moabite ascent, the going up to Luhith, where fugitives wept as they fled Moab's destruction.
BiblicalSignificance: Luhith is the weeping ascent of Moab's fugitives.

Name: Lycaonia
Description: The plain of Lystra and Derbe, where Paul was worshipped as a god, then stoned, then returned to strengthen the disciples.
BiblicalSignificance: Lycaonia saw both extremes of missionary life in one journey: worship, then stones.

Name: Lycia
Description: The coastal province where Paul's ship changed course at Myra on the voyage to Rome.
BiblicalSignificance: Lycia is a waypoint on Paul's last voyage, where the journey to Caesar changed ships.

Name: Lydia
Description: Called Lud in the Old Testament, a land of warriors and traders in western Asia Minor. Lud appears among the nations in Ezekiel's oracles and among the peoples who will hear of God's glory.
BiblicalSignificance: Lydia is one more distant nation drawn into the reach of God's word, from the prophets to the ends of the earth.

Name: Lystra
Description: A Lycaonian town where Paul healed a lame man, was hailed as a god, then was stoned and left for dead, and where Timothy joined him.
BiblicalSignificance: Lystra is where missionary glory and missionary suffering met in a single visit.

Name: Macedonia
Description: The Roman province of northern Greece, entered after Paul's vision of the Macedonian man, home of Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea.
BiblicalSignificance: Macedonia is where the gospel first entered Europe, answering a night vision with a continent.

Name: Magdala
ModernLocation: Migdal, western shore of the Sea of Galilee
Description: A fishing town on the Sea of Galilee's western shore, where Jesus came after feeding the four thousand.
BiblicalSignificance: Magdala is a landing point in Jesus' Galilean ministry, on the road between miracles.

Name: Magog
Description: A northern land named among Japheth's sons and, in Ezekiel, the land of Gog, prince of Meshech and Tubal. Its location is not stated in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Magog is prophecy's far north, a name of dread left deliberately unmapped.

Name: Mahanaim
Description: The place where Jacob met the angels of God and named it "two camps," later a Levitical city and David's refuge during Absalom's revolt.
BiblicalSignificance: Mahanaim is where Jacob saw God's camp beside his own, and where David waited while Absalom's rebellion burned.

Name: Makheloth
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Makkedah
Description: A Canaanite royal city where the five Amorite kings hid in a cave after the battle of Gibeon and were executed.
BiblicalSignificance: Makkedah's cave is where Joshua shut the five kings in with great stones until the battle was won.

Name: Maon
