Description: A Judahite town in the wilderness where David hid from Saul, who was called away by a Philistine raid at the last moment.
BiblicalSignificance: Maon is the wilderness town where Saul nearly closed his hand on David, and the rock of divisions parted them.

Name: Marah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The place of bitter waters made sweet when Moses cast in the tree God showed him. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Mareshah
Description: A fortified city of Judah where Asa defeated Zerah the Ethiopian's vast army in the Valley of Zephathah.
BiblicalSignificance: Mareshah is where Asa's prayer met an army of a million, and God gave the victory.

Name: Medeba
Description: A Moabite city on the plateau, named in the conquest lists and in the oracles against Moab, and the scene of Ammon's muster against David.
BiblicalSignificance: Medeba is the plateau city where Ammon mustered against David.

Name: Media
Description: The kingdom of the Medes, joined with Persia under Cyrus. The "law of the Medes and Persians" could not be changed, and it was under a Median king that Daniel was thrown to the lions and delivered.
BiblicalSignificance: Media shows that no unchangeable human law can stand against God when He purposes to deliver His servant.

Name: Megiddo
Description: A fortress city guarding the Jezreel pass, allotted to Manasseh, fortified by Solomon, where kings Ahaziah and Josiah died.
BiblicalSignificance: Megiddo is the crossroads city of armies, from Deborah's battle to Josiah's death, and the namesake of Armageddon.

Name: Melita
Description: The island, called Malta today, where Paul's ship wrecked, a viper bit him harmlessly, and Publius' father was healed.
BiblicalSignificance: Melita is where shipwreck became witness, and island kindness met apostolic healing.

Name: Memphis
Description: Called Noph in the King James Version, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt, named in the prophets' oracles against Egypt.
BiblicalSignificance: Memphis, capital of the old kingdom, stands judged with the idols it trusted.

Name: Meshech
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally Asia Minor or the Black Sea region
Description: A northern people and land, joined with Tubal in the Table of Nations, in Tyre's trade, and in Ezekiel's oracle.
BiblicalSignificance: Meshech, named beside Tubal, belongs to the far north that prophecy gathers against God's people.

Name: Mesopotamia
ModernLocation: Iraq, between the Tigris and Euphrates
Description: The land between the rivers, Abraham's homeland, whose people were present at Pentecost.
BiblicalSignificance: Mesopotamia is where the patriarchs began, and whose sons heard the gospel in their own tongue at Pentecost.

Name: Migdol
ModernLocation: Unknown; on the west shore of the Red Sea, Egypt
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. A landmark named beside Pi-hahiroth in the crossing account; the same name later marks an Egyptian frontier town. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Miletus
Description: The great port of Asia where Paul, hurrying to Jerusalem, summoned the Ephesian elders and wept his farewell.
BiblicalSignificance: Miletus is where Paul's farewell to the elders warned of wolves and commended them to God.

Name: Minni
Description: A kingdom named with Ararat and Ashkenaz in Jeremiah's summons against Babylon. Its exact place is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Minni is one of the highland kingdoms called to God's muster against Babylon.

Name: Mithcah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Mitylene
Description: The chief city of Lesbos, where Paul's ship paused on the hurried voyage to Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Mitylene is one more island pause on Paul's race to Pentecost in Jerusalem.

Name: Moab
ModernLocation: Jordan, east of the Dead Sea
Description: The kingdom east of the Dead Sea, descended from Lot. Moab opposed Israel in the wilderness, oppressed Israel in the days of the judges, and is judged at length by Isaiah and Jeremiah; yet Ruth the Moabitess became the ancestress of David.
BiblicalSignificance: Moab holds both warning and grace: a nation under judgment, and a Moabite woman grafted into the line of the Messiah.
KeyScriptures: Numbers 21:29; Isaiah 15:1; Jeremiah 48:1; Numbers 22:1; Ruth 1:1; Deuteronomy 34:5

Name: Moseroth
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Mount Ebal
ModernLocation: Mount Ebal, near Nablus, West Bank
Description: The mountain of the curse above Shechem, where Joshua built an altar of uncut stones and wrote the law.
BiblicalSignificance: Ebal is where Israel heard the curses of disobedience and built the altar of the covenant.

Name: Mount Ephraim
ModernLocation: Hill country of Ephraim, central Israel
Description: The central hill country settled by Ephraim, home of Joshua at Timnath-serah and of Micah's idols and the Levite's concubine.
BiblicalSignificance: Mount Ephraim is the heartland of the central tribes, the hill country of Joshua's inheritance.

Name: Mount Gerizim
ModernLocation: Mount Gerizim, near Nablus, West Bank
Description: The mountain of blessing above Shechem, where half the tribes stood to pronounce the blessings of the law.
BiblicalSignificance: Gerizim is the mountain of blessing, paired with Ebal's curses, where Israel renewed the covenant.

Name: Mount Gilboa
Description: The ridge above the Jezreel Valley where Saul and Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines.
BiblicalSignificance: Gilboa is where David's lament fell: "Tell it not in Gath," for the shield of Saul was cast away there.

Name: Mount Hermon
Description: The snow-capped northern mountain, the landmark of Israel's northern border, whose dew became a picture of brotherly unity.
BiblicalSignificance: Hermon is the high north, whose dew falls on Zion in the psalm of brethren dwelling together.

Name: Mount Hor
Description: The mountain on Edom's border where Aaron died and Eleazar took his priestly garments, a station on the wilderness journey.
BiblicalSignificance: Hor is where the first high priest died in sight of the land, and the priesthood passed to his son.

Name: Mount Moriah
Description: The mountain where Abraham bound Isaac and where Solomon later built the temple.
BiblicalSignificance: Moriah is where God provided the ram, and where the temple rose on the same ground of provision.

Name: Mount Nebo
Description: The mountain in Moab from which Moses saw the Promised Land before he died, and where he was buried in the valley below.
BiblicalSignificance: Nebo is where Moses saw the land he would not enter, and where his eyes stayed undimmed to the end.

Name: Mount of Olives
Description: The ridge east of Jerusalem, named in David's flight and in Zechariah's prophecy, where Jesus taught, prayed, and ascended.
BiblicalSignificance: The Mount of Olives frames the end of Jesus' ministry: His teaching, His agony, and His ascension to heaven.
RelatedEvents: The Ascension; Triumphal Entry; Jesus Prays in Gethsemane

Name: Mount Pisgah
Description: The summit of the Abarim range, the lookout from which Moses viewed the whole land, also named for the Pisgah region.
BiblicalSignificance: Pisgah is the viewing height of Moses' last look at Canaan, from the Arabah to the western sea.

Name: Mount Seir
Description: The mountain of Seir, home of the Horites and later of Esau's descendants, the land of Edom. Abram's war reached its slopes.
BiblicalSignificance: Seir is Esau's mountain, the land of the brother who sold his birthright.

Name: Mount Shapher
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Mount Tabor
Description: The dome-shaped mountain above the Jezreel Valley where Deborah and Barak mustered ten thousand men against Sisera.
BiblicalSignificance: Tabor is the mustering mountain of Deborah's victory, where the tribes gathered before the Kishon swept the enemy away.

Name: Mount Zion
Description: The hill of Jerusalem where David brought the ark and where the temple stood, the mountain God chose for His name.
BiblicalSignificance: Zion is the mountain of God's dwelling, the city of the great King, and the hope of all the earth's praise.

Name: Myra
Description: A city of Lycia where Paul, now a prisoner, boarded an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy.
BiblicalSignificance: Myra is where Paul's voyage to Rome found its ship, an Alexandrian grain carrier.

Name: Mysia
Description: A district of northwest Asia Minor which Paul passed through on his way to Troas and Macedonia.
BiblicalSignificance: Mysia is a road on Paul's second journey, where the Spirit closed one door and opened Europe.

Name: Nain
Description: A small town in Galilee where Jesus met a funeral procession and raised a widow's only son.
BiblicalSignificance: Nain shows Jesus' compassion interrupting grief itself, and fear and glory fell on all who saw it.

Name: Neapolis
Description: The port of Philippi, where Paul first landed in Europe after the Macedonian vision.
BiblicalSignificance: Neapolis is Europe's doorstep: Paul's first European landfall.

Name: Nebo
Description: A Moabite city named in the conquest lists and in the oracles against Moab. It is distinct from Mount Nebo, from which Moses viewed Canaan.
BiblicalSignificance: Nebo the city must not be confused with Nebo the mountain: Scripture names both.

Name: Negev
ModernLocation: Southern Israel, from Beersheba toward the Sinai
Description: The dry southern hill country of Canaan, travelled by Abram and Isaac and later settled by Judah and Simeon.
BiblicalSignificance: The Negev is where the patriarchs sojourned and where Israel first approached the Promised Land from the south.

Name: Nile
Description: The river of Egypt, turned to blood in the first plague, named in the prophets' oracles against Egypt and in the story of Moses' basket.
BiblicalSignificance: The Nile is Egypt's life and Egypt's judgment, bloodied and then restored.

Name: Oboth
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: On
Description: The Egyptian city of the sun-god, home of Joseph's father-in-law the priest Potiphera, and named by Ezekiel among the cities judged.
BiblicalSignificance: On is Egypt's priestly city, joined to Joseph's family by marriage.

Name: Ono
Description: A Benjamite town in the plain where Sanballat and Geshem tried to lure Nehemiah to a meeting to do him harm.
BiblicalSignificance: Ono is the plain of the trap Nehemiah refused: "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down."

Name: Paddan Aram
Description: The "plain of Aram" where Abraham's kin lived, around Haran. Jacob fled here to Laban, married Leah and Rachel, and served twenty years before returning to Canaan.
BiblicalSignificance: Paddan Aram is the place of waiting and wrestling: God formed Jacob's family far from home before bringing them back.

Name: Pamphylia
Description: The coastal plain of southern Asia Minor, where Paul landed at Perga and where John Mark left the party.
BiblicalSignificance: Pamphylia is where the first missionary team thinned, and where the word still went on.

Name: Paphos
Description: The western capital of Cyprus where Paul confronted the sorcerer Elymas and the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed.
BiblicalSignificance: Paphos is where a Roman governor believed, and the mission turned from a Jewish audience to the Gentile world.

Name: Parvaim
Description: A gold-bearing land named once, as the source of the gold overlaying the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple.
BiblicalSignificance: Parvaim is remembered for one thing only: its gold covered the holiest room on earth.

Name: Patara
Description: A Lycian port where Paul changed ships, leaving the coastal vessel for one bound straight to Phoenicia.
BiblicalSignificance: Patara is where Paul's voyage turned from island-hopping to the open run for Tyre.

Name: Pathros
Description: Upper Egypt, the southern land of the Nile, named as a place of both judgment and promised return for scattered Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: Pathros shows God gathering His people from the far south as surely as from Babylon.

Name: Penuel
Description: The Transjordan town by the Jabbok ford where Jacob wrestled with God, later fortified by Jeroboam.
BiblicalSignificance: Penuel is where Jacob wrestled until dawn and walked away limping with a new name, Israel.

Name: Peor
Description: The mountain in Moab from which Balaam looked over Israel and blessed instead of cursing, for the third time.
BiblicalSignificance: Peor is the mountain of the blessing that would not be a curse.

Name: Perga
Description: The capital of Pamphylia where Paul landed on the first journey and where John Mark departed for Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Perga is where the first team lost a member, and where Paul later preached on the way back.

Name: Pergamos
Description: The old capital of Asia, addressed in Revelation as the church where Satan's seat was, yet which held fast Christ's name.
BiblicalSignificance: Pergamos is the church under pressure, praised for holding fast where the enemy enthroned himself.

Name: Persia
Description: The empire that succeeded Babylon. Cyrus's decree let the Jews return from exile, and later Persian kings figure in the stories of Esther, Ezra, and Nehemiah.
BiblicalSignificance: Persia shows God steering the greatest empire on earth to serve His people's return and the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Name: Pharpar
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally a Damascus river, Syria
Description: The second river of Damascus named by Naaman, beside Abana. Its exact course is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Pharpar, with Abana, is the pride of Damascus set against the Jordan.

Name: Phenice
Description: The KJV name for the Phoenician coast, where believers scattered by Stephen's persecution preached, and through which Paul traveled.
BiblicalSignificance: Phenice is where the scattered church first carried the word beyond Jerusalem's shadow.

Name: Philadelphia
Description: A city of Asia on the road east, addressed in Revelation as the church of the open door, kept faithful with little strength.
BiblicalSignificance: Philadelphia is the faithful little church, given an open door no one can shut.

Name: Philistia
ModernLocation: Southern coastal plain of Canaan, modern Gaza Strip and southern Israel
Description: The coastal territory of the Philistines and their five cities, Israel's near-constant rival from the judges through David.
BiblicalSignificance: Philistia is the stage of the Samson stories, the capture of the ark, and David's long wars before he subdued it.

Name: Phoenix
Description: A Cretan haven, spelled Phenice in the KJV, which Paul's ship hoped to reach to winter, but never did.
BiblicalSignificance: Phoenix is the harbor that got away: the goal of a voyage the wind refused.

Name: Phrygia
Description: The inland province Paul crossed on his second and third journeys, strengthening the disciples.
BiblicalSignificance: Phrygia is crossed twice by Paul, a land of strengthening rather than headlines.

Name: Pi-beseth
Description: An Egyptian city named by Ezekiel among the cities that would fall by the sword.
BiblicalSignificance: Pi-beseth is a single-verse city, named in judgment and no more.

Name: Pi-hahiroth
ModernLocation: Unknown; on the west shore of the Red Sea, Egypt
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The camp between Migdol and the sea, where Israel was trapped before the waters parted. Nearby landmarks named in the crossing account are Migdol and Baal-zephon. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Pisidia
Description: The rugged inland region Paul crossed to reach Antioch in Pisidia and preach in its synagogue.
BiblicalSignificance: Pisidia is the hard road to Antioch's synagogue, where Paul preached Christ from the prophets.

Name: Pison
Description: The first river of Eden, compassing the land of Havilah where there is gold. Its course is not identified in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Pison is Eden's gold river, named and left unmapped.

Name: Pithom
Description: One of the treasure cities Pharaoh made Israel build in bondage, named in Exodus alongside Raamses.
BiblicalSignificance: Pithom is a city built by slaves, a monument to bondage.

Name: Pontus
ModernLocation: Northern Turkey along the Black Sea
Description: The Black Sea province whose people were at Pentecost, and from which Aquila came to Corinth.
BiblicalSignificance: Pontus connects Pentecost's crowd to Paul's Corinthian workshop through Aquila.

Name: Pool of Bethesda
Description: A pool in Jerusalem surrounded by five porches, where the sick waited for the stirring of the water; Jesus healed a man there who had been infirm thirty-eight years.
BiblicalSignificance: Bethesda shows Jesus healing on the Sabbath and claiming authority over the law's own holy day.

Name: Pool of Siloam
ModernLocation: Jerusalem, south end of the City of David
Description: The pool fed by Hezekiah's tunnel, called Shiloah in Isaiah and Nehemiah; Jesus sent the man born blind to wash there, and he came back seeing.
BiblicalSignificance: Siloam links Hezekiah's waterworks to Jesus' sign: the sent one gives sight to the blind.

Name: Ptolemais
Description: The port city called Accho in Judges, where Paul spent a day with the brethren on his final journey to Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Ptolemais is a one-day pause on Paul's last free road to Jerusalem.

Name: Punon
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with Faynan, Jordan
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. A mining region of the Arabah, later known for its copper works. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Puteoli
Description: The great Italian port where Paul landed, found brethren, and stayed seven days on the way to Rome.
BiblicalSignificance: Puteoli is where Italy welcomed Paul with a week's hospitality before the road to Rome.

Name: Raamah
Description: An Arabian trading land named among Cush's sons and among the merchants of Tyre, dealing in spices, precious stones, and gold.
BiblicalSignificance: Raamah is one more Arabian merchant land whose wealth flowed to Tyre, and whose judgment the prophets foresee.

Name: Rabbah
Description: The capital of Ammon, where David's army besieged the city while he stayed in Jerusalem, and where Og's great iron bedstead was kept.
BiblicalSignificance: Rabbah is Ammon's capital, the city of David's siege and his great sin.

Name: Rameses
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the Nile Delta, Egypt
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The starting point of the Exodus, the store city Israel left on the night of the Passover. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Ramoth-gilead
Description: A city of refuge in Gad, fought over by Israel and Aram, where Ahab died in battle and Jehu was anointed king.
BiblicalSignificance: Ramoth-gilead is where Ahab fell disguised in battle and where Jehu was anointed to end Ahab's house.

Name: Red Sea
ModernLocation: Red Sea, between Egypt and Arabia
Description: The sea God parted for Israel's escape from Egypt and closed over Pharaoh's army, also called the Sea of Reeds.
BiblicalSignificance: The Red Sea is the water of deliverance, where Israel walked dry-shod and sang the song of Moses.
KeyScriptures: Exodus 14:21; Exodus 15:1; Numbers 33:10; Exodus 15:4; 1 Kings 9:26; Acts 7:36; Hebrews 11:29
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea

Name: Rehob
Description: An Aramean city and kingdom, Beth-rehob, near Hamath, whose king allied with Ammon against David.
BiblicalSignificance: Rehob is the Aramean ally that marched against David and lost.

Name: Rehoboth
Description: An Assyrian city named in the Table of Nations. It is distinct from the well Rehoboth that Isaac dug in Genesis 26.
BiblicalSignificance: Rehoboth of Assyria must not be confused with Isaac's well: Scripture reuses the name.

Name: Rephidim
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. The camp where water came from the rock and Amalek was defeated while Moses' hands were held up. The name Meribah belongs to the quarrel here, not to a separate place. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Resen
Description: A great city of Assyria named between Nineveh and Calah in the Table of Nations. Its site is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Resen is a great-city name whose stones have not been certainly found.

Name: Rhegium
Description: The toe of Italy, where Paul's ship came after Syracuse and waited a day for a south wind.
BiblicalSignificance: Rhegium is where the south wind finally came, and the ship ran for Puteoli.

Name: Rhodes
Description: The great island of the southeastern Aegean, where Paul's ship came after Coos.
BiblicalSignificance: Rhodes is another island on the road to Jerusalem, named in the voyage list.

Name: Riblah
Description: The Syrian town where Pharaoh Necho imprisoned Jehoahaz, and where Nebuchadnezzar blinded Zedekiah after slaying his sons before his eyes.
BiblicalSignificance: Riblah is where Judah's kingship ended in chains and darkness.

Name: Rimmon-parez
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the wilderness of Paran
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Rissah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Rithmah
ModernLocation: Unknown; in the wilderness of Paran
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: River Arnon
Description: The deep gorge river forming Moab's northern border, crossed by Israel after defeating Sihon.
BiblicalSignificance: Arnon is the border river Israel crossed into the Amorite kingdom, and the line of Moab's lament.

Name: River Jabbok
Description: The tributary of the Jordan that Jacob crossed after wrestling with God, marking the boundary of Gilead and Ammon.
BiblicalSignificance: Jabbok is the ford of the wrestling night, where Jacob became Israel.

Name: River of Egypt
Description: The southwestern boundary stream of the promised land, named in the covenant with Abram and in the borders of Numbers and Kings.
BiblicalSignificance: The River of Egypt is the promised land's southern edge.

Name: Salamis
Description: The eastern port of Cyprus where Paul and Barnabas first preached in the island's synagogues.
BiblicalSignificance: Salamis is where the first missionary journey's island work began, synagogue by synagogue.

Name: Salim
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with Salim near Nablus or the Jordan Valley
Description: The place near Aenon where John baptized; not the Salem of Genesis, but a distinct site in the Jordan region.
BiblicalSignificance: Salim anchors John's late baptizing ministry in a real, watered place.

Name: Salmone
Description: The eastern cape of Crete under which Paul's ship sailed, seeking shelter from the wind.
BiblicalSignificance: Salmone is the lee shore of Crete, the last easy sailing before the storm.

Name: Samos
Description: An Aegean island where Paul's ship tarried a day on the voyage to Miletus.
BiblicalSignificance: Samos is a one-day stop on Paul's hurried road to Jerusalem.

Name: Samothracia
Description: A mountainous Aegean island where Paul's ship spent a night on the crossing to Neapolis.
BiblicalSignificance: Samothracia is a night's anchorage on the crossing into Europe.

Name: Sardis
Description: The old Lydian capital, addressed in Revelation as a church with a name that it lived, but which was dead.
BiblicalSignificance: Sardis is the wake-up church: reputation is not life, and a few undefiled garments remain.

Name: School of Tyrannus
Description: The lecture hall in Ephesus, named for Tyrannus, where Paul reasoned daily for two years so that all Asia heard the word.
BiblicalSignificance: The School of Tyrannus is where daily reasoning filled a province with the word of the Lord.

Name: Sea of Chinnereth
Description: The freshwater lake of the north, called Chinnereth in the Old Testament, bordering Naphtali and the tribal lands. Called the Sea of Galilee in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Chinnereth is the northern sea of the tribal allotments, the lake that would later hear the preaching of Jesus.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Joshua; Jesus; Simon Peter; Andrew; Matthew; Thomas
RelatedEvents: Jesus Calms the Storm; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Name: Seba
Description: A distant southern land named among the peoples who bring gifts to the King, alongside Sheba and Tarshish.
BiblicalSignificance: Seba is one of the far-off names that promise a King whose reign outruns every map.

Name: Sela
Description: The rock city of Edom, taken by Amaziah who called it Joktheel, and named in Isaiah's call to Moab to send lambs to Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Sela is the rock city, taken by Amaziah and traditionally called Petra.

Name: Sepharvaim
Description: A Mesopotamian city whose people were settled in Samaria, and whose gods the Assyrian taunt named against Jerusalem.
BiblicalSignificance: Sepharvaim is a city whose gods could not save it, and whose people were moved into Samaria.

Name: Sharon
ModernLocation: Coastal plain north of Joppa, Israel
Description: The fertile coastal plain stretching north from Joppa toward Carmel, famed for its flowers and pastures. Called Saron in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Sharon's beauty became a picture of restoration: Isaiah promises the wilderness will blossom like Sharon.
KeyScriptures: 1 Chronicles 27:29; Song of Solomon 2:1; Isaiah 35:2; Acts 9:35
RelatedBooks: 1 Chronicles; Song of Solomon; Isaiah; Acts

Name: Sheba
Description: A wealthy southern kingdom famed for gold, spices, and precious stones. Its queen travelled to test Solomon with hard questions and marvelled at his wisdom.
BiblicalSignificance: Sheba shows that wisdom, when it is God's, draws seekers from the ends of the earth.

Name: Shephelah
ModernLocation: Low foothills between the coastal plain and the Judean hills, Israel
Description: The rolling foothills west of the Judean mountains, a contested borderland between Israel and Philistia where many battles were fought.
BiblicalSignificance: Border country: the Shephelah saw the battles of Aijalon, Elah, and the Philistine wars of Saul and David.

Name: Shinar
Description: The plain of southern Mesopotamia, the land of Babel and of Nimrod's first cities. Here men built the tower of Babel, and here later Judah's treasures were carried in exile.
BiblicalSignificance: Shinar is where human pride first organised itself against heaven, and where God scattered it.

Name: Shittim
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the Tell el-Hammam area, Jordan Valley, Jordan
Description: The last camp of Israel east of the Jordan, where Israel sinned with Moab and from which Joshua sent the spies to Jericho.
BiblicalSignificance: Shittim is the camp of the last temptation before the crossing, and the launching place of the conquest.

Name: Shunem
Description: An Issachar town where the Philistines camped before Gilboa, and home of the Shunammite woman who hosted Elisha.
BiblicalSignificance: Shunem is where Elisha raised the Shunammite's son, and where the Philistine army gathered before Saul's last battle.

Name: Sibmah
Description: A Moabite vineyard city named in the conquest lists and lamented in Isaiah and Jeremiah for its vines.
BiblicalSignificance: Sibmah is Moab's vine city, wept over in the oracle.

Name: Sidon
Description: The ancient Phoenician seaport, called Zidon in the King James Version. Mother city of Tyre's trade, home of Jezebel, and a city named in the prophets' oracles and in Jesus' teaching.
BiblicalSignificance: Sidon, older than Tyre and judged beside it, heard Jesus say that Tyre and Sidon would have repented at His works.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:15; Judges 1:31; 1 Kings 5:6; Ezekiel 27:8; Matthew 15:21; Acts 27:3
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Judges; 1 Kings; Ezekiel; Matthew; Acts

Name: Sihor
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally a Nile branch, Egypt
Description: A river of Egypt named as a border of the promised land and as the waters of Egypt in Jeremiah's rebuke.
BiblicalSignificance: Sihor is Egypt's dark water, named at the border and in rebuke.

Name: Smyrna
Description: A wealthy port of Asia, addressed in Revelation as a church that would suffer poverty and prison yet remain faithful.
BiblicalSignificance: Smyrna is the suffering church, promised the crown of life for faithfulness unto death.

Name: Socoh
Description: A Judahite town in the Elah Valley, the Philistine camp town when Goliath challenged Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: Socoh is the town beside the valley where David faced Goliath.

Name: Sodom
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southern Dead Sea region
Description: The chief city of the plain where Lot settled, notorious for its wickedness, destroyed by fire from heaven.
BiblicalSignificance: Sodom is the Bible's standing warning of judgment, and the backdrop of Abraham's intercession for the righteous.

Name: Solomon's Porch
ModernLocation: Jerusalem, eastern side of the temple precinct
Description: The covered colonnade on the temple's east side where Jesus walked and where the early church gathered daily.
BiblicalSignificance: Solomon's Porch became the early church's meeting place, where signs and wonders drew all Jerusalem's attention.

Name: Spain
Description: The western edge of the empire, where Paul hoped to preach after Rome, though Scripture does not record the visit.
BiblicalSignificance: Spain is Paul's unfinished horizon: the gospel's westward hope, stated but not yet told.

Name: Succoth
ModernLocation: Tell Deir Alla area, Jordan Valley, Jordan
Description: The Transjordan town where Jacob built booths for his cattle, later a city whose elders Gideon disciplined; the name also belongs to Israel's first wilderness encampment in Egypt, a distinct place sharing the name.
BiblicalSignificance: Succoth is where Jacob paused on the way home, and where Gideon taught a town that refused bread to his hungry men.

Name: Sychar
Description: A Samaritan city near Jacob's well, where Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman and many believed.
BiblicalSignificance: Sychar is where Jesus crossed ethnic and moral barriers, and a whole town came to faith through one woman's testimony.

Name: Syracuse
Description: The great Sicilian port where Paul's ship tarried three days on the voyage to Rome.
BiblicalSignificance: Syracuse is a three-day pause on the final leg to Rome.

Name: Taanach
Description: A Canaanite royal city near Megiddo, allotted to Manasseh and given to the Levites.
BiblicalSignificance: Taanach is named in Deborah's song as the place where the kings of Canaan fought and took no spoil.

Name: Tadmor
Description: The desert oasis city Solomon built in the wilderness, on the trade road between the Euphrates and the sea.
BiblicalSignificance: Tadmor is Solomon's desert outpost, a city raised where the trade roads meet the sand.

Name: Tahath
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Tahpanhes
Description: The Egyptian border fortress where Jeremiah was carried after Jerusalem's fall, and where he buried stones and foretold Nebuchadnezzar's throne set over Egypt.
BiblicalSignificance: Tahpanhes is where the prophet was dragged in disobedience, and still prophesied.

Name: Tarah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Tarsus
Description: The Cilician city where Paul was born a Roman citizen and a Pharisee, and to which he returned after his conversion.
BiblicalSignificance: Tarsus gave the apostle to the Gentiles his citizenship, his learning, and his sending church's reach.

Name: Tekoa
Description: A Judahite town south of Bethlehem, home of the prophet Amos and of the wise woman who pleaded for Absalom.
BiblicalSignificance: Tekoa is Amos's home among the herdsmen, and the town whose wise woman spoke truth to David.

Name: Telassar
Description: A Mesopotamian city named in the Assyrian boast, home of the children of Eden whom Assyria conquered.
BiblicalSignificance: Telassar is a conquered city in an empire's boast.

Name: Tema
Description: An Arabian oasis town whose people brought water to the fugitives of Kedar, and whose caravans Job's friends watched for in vain.
BiblicalSignificance: Tema is the desert oasis that gives water to the fleeing, and a byword for help that does not come.

Name: Teman
Description: A region and city of Edom famed for wisdom, named in the oracles against Edom and as the place from which God comes in Habakkuk.
BiblicalSignificance: Teman is Edom's wise region, whose wisdom could not save it.

Name: Thebes
Description: Called No in the King James Version, the great southern capital of Egypt and centre of Amun worship, named by Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Nahum.
BiblicalSignificance: Thebes, no less than Nineveh, is held up as a city whose greatness could not save it.

Name: Three Taverns
ModernLocation: Near Rome, Italy (on the Appian Way)
Description: A roadside station on the Appian Way where another party of Roman brethren met Paul on his approach to the city.
BiblicalSignificance: Three Taverns is the second welcome on the Appian Way, and Paul took courage twice.

Name: Thyatira
Description: A trade city of Asia, home of Lydia the purple-seller, addressed in Revelation for its love and service and its tolerance of Jezebel.
BiblicalSignificance: Thyatira joins Lydia's conversion to Revelation's warning: love without discernment is not enough.

Name: Tiberias
ModernLocation: Tiberias, western shore of the Sea of Galilee
Description: Herod Antipas' lakeside capital, whose boats came looking for Jesus after the feeding of the five thousand.
BiblicalSignificance: Tiberias is the city that gives the Sea of Galilee its other name, the Sea of Tiberias.

Name: Tibhath
Description: A city of Hadadezer from which David took much brass for the temple. Its parallel name in Samuel is Betah.
BiblicalSignificance: Tibhath gave its brass to the house of God.

Name: Timnath-serah
ModernLocation: Khirbet Tibneh, hill country of Ephraim, Israel
Description: The town in Mount Ephraim that Israel gave to Joshua as his inheritance, where he lived and was buried.
BiblicalSignificance: Timnath-serah is Joshua's own town, the inheritance of the conqueror who asked for a hill town.

Name: Timnath
Description: A Philistine-border town where Samson married and posed his riddle, and where Judah's road to Timnath ran in Genesis.
BiblicalSignificance: Timnath is Samson's wedding town, where the lion, the honey, and the riddle unfolded.

Name: Tirzah
Description: An early capital of the northern kingdom, praised for beauty in the Song of Solomon, seat of kings from Jeroboam to Omri.
BiblicalSignificance: Tirzah was Israel's first royal city after the division, beautiful and brief, before Omri moved the capital to Samaria.

Name: Tob
Description: A Transjordan land where Jephthah took refuge from his brothers, and whose men later fought as Ammonite allies against David.
BiblicalSignificance: Tob is the outlaw's refuge that became a judge's launching place.

Name: Togarmah
Description: A northern house named in the Table of Nations, trading horses and mules with Tyre, and marching with Gog in Ezekiel.
BiblicalSignificance: Togarmah is one of the horse-trading northlands drawn into both commerce and prophecy.

Name: Tower of Siloam
ModernLocation: Jerusalem, near the Pool of Siloam
Description: A tower in Jerusalem whose fall killed eighteen people, which Jesus cited to warn His hearers to repent.
BiblicalSignificance: The Tower of Siloam is Jesus' lesson that tragedy is not a measure of guilt, but a call to repentance for all.

Name: Trachonitis
Description: A rugged volcanic district east of the Jordan, part of Philip the tetrarch's territory.
BiblicalSignificance: Trachonitis is named in Luke's careful dating of John the Baptist's ministry.

Name: Troas
Description: The port of northwest Asia Minor where Paul received the Macedonian vision and where he later raised Eutychus.
BiblicalSignificance: Troas is the door to Europe: a night vision there turned the gospel westward.

Name: Trogyllium
Description: A promontory and anchorage on the Asian coast where Paul's ship waited before Miletus.
BiblicalSignificance: Trogyllium is a waiting place on the voyage, named once and never again.

Name: Tubal
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally Asia Minor or the Black Sea region
Description: A northern people and land named in the Table of Nations, among Tyre's traders, and in Ezekiel's oracle against Gog.
BiblicalSignificance: Tubal stands at the northern edge of the map, among the nations gathered in the last battle.

Name: Ulai
Description: The river in Elam, beside Susa, where Daniel saw the vision of the ram and the goat.
BiblicalSignificance: Ulai is the river of Daniel's vision, in the province of Elam.

Name: Uzal
Description: A Joktanite land in southern Arabia, traditionally identified with the region of Sana'a in Yemen.
BiblicalSignificance: Uzal is a single-verse name, kept honestly thin: Scripture names it and says no more.

Name: Valley of Achor
ModernLocation: Wadi el-Qelt area, near Jericho, Israel
Description: The valley where Achan was stoned for taking devoted spoil, later promised as a door of hope.
BiblicalSignificance: Achor is the valley of trouble turned to a door of hope, where judgment and restoration meet.

Name: Valley of Berachah
Description: The valley of blessing where Jehoshaphat's army praised God after the enemy armies destroyed each other.
BiblicalSignificance: Berachah is the valley where praise became the victory, and the spoil took three days to gather.

Name: Valley of Elah
Description: The valley between Socoh and Azekah where the armies of Israel and Philistia faced each other and David slew Goliath.
BiblicalSignificance: Elah is the valley of the giant's challenge, where a shepherd boy's stone ended forty days of defiance.

Name: Valley of Hinnom
ModernLocation: Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem, Israel
Description: The valley south of Jerusalem where children were sacrificed to Molech, later defiled by Josiah and used as a symbol of judgment.
BiblicalSignificance: Hinnom, Gehenna, became the Bible's picture of the place of fire prepared for the wicked.

Name: Valley of Jehoshaphat
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem, Israel
Description: The valley named in Joel as the place where God will gather the nations for judgment.
BiblicalSignificance: Jehoshaphat is the valley of decision, where Joel saw all nations gathered before the Lord.

Name: Valley of Jezreel
Description: The broad fertile valley between the hills of Samaria and Galilee, Israel's breadbasket and battlefield.
BiblicalSignificance: Jezreel is the valley of harvest and of war, from Gideon's Midianites to the blood of Naboth's vineyard.

Name: Valley of Rephaim
Description: The valley of giants southwest of Jerusalem, where David twice defeated the Philistines, once at the sound of marching in the mulberry trees.
BiblicalSignificance: Rephaim is where David learned to wait for the sound of God's going before him in the trees.

Name: Valley of Siddim
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southern Dead Sea region
Description: The valley of bitumen pits where the kings of the plain met the kings of the east in battle, and where Lot was captured.
BiblicalSignificance: The valley of Siddim is where Abram first went to war to rescue Lot, defeating Chedorlaomer's alliance.

Name: Valley of Sorek
Description: The valley of the choice vine where Samson loved Delilah, on the border of Judah and Philistia.
BiblicalSignificance: Sorek is the valley of the vine where Samson's strength was sold for silver.

Name: Waters of Merom
Description: The waters of the northern lake where Jabin's coalition camped and Joshua fell on them suddenly.
BiblicalSignificance: Merom is where Joshua's sudden attack broke the northern kings beside the waters.

Name: Wilderness of Judah
ModernLocation: Barren hills east of Bethlehem toward the Dead Sea, Israel
Description: The rugged desert east of the Judean hills where David hid from Saul and where John the Baptist would later preach.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness of Judah is David's refuge and the psalmist's thirsty land: "my soul thirsteth for thee in a dry land."

Name: Wilderness of Paran
ModernLocation: Desert south of Canaan, modern Negev-Sinai region
Description: The great desert where Ishmael grew up and where Israel camped after leaving Sinai, sending the spies into Canaan from its edge.
BiblicalSignificance: Paran is the wilderness of waiting and failure: from here the spies went up, and here the people refused to enter the land.

Name: Wilderness of Sin
ModernLocation: Desert between Elim and Sinai, modern Sinai Peninsula
Description: The wilderness Israel crossed after Elim, where God first gave manna and where the people grumbled about bread.
BiblicalSignificance: Sin is where daily bread from heaven began: manna fell here, teaching Israel to trust God one day at a time.

Name: Wilderness of Zin
ModernLocation: Desert south of Canaan around Kadesh, modern Negev
Description: The desert wilderness bordering Edom where Israel camped at Kadesh, and from which the spies entered the land.
BiblicalSignificance: Zin is the wilderness of Kadesh: Miriam died here, Moses struck the rock here, and the spies set out from here.

Name: Zalmonah
Description: One of the stations on Israel's wilderness journey, named in the Numbers 33 itinerary. No further detail is recorded beyond the journey account.
BiblicalSignificance: The wilderness stations trace the route God led Israel from Egypt to the Plains of Moab.

Name: Zarephath
Description: The Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon where Elijah was fed by a widow whose oil and meal did not run out, and which Obadiah names as a place of returning exiles. Called Sarepta in the New Testament.
BiblicalSignificance: Zarephath is where a Gentile widow fed the prophet, and the barrel did not fail.

Name: Zeboiim
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southern Dead Sea region
Description: One of the cities of the plain, destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah.
BiblicalSignificance: Zeboiim stands in the prophetic memory as a city God overthrew, yet one He remembers with compassion.

Name: Ziklag
Description: A Philistine town given to David by Achish, burned by Amalekites while David was away, then recovered with all captives.
BiblicalSignificance: Ziklag is where David's men nearly stoned him and where he found strength in God and recovered all.

Name: Ziph
Description: A Judahite town whose people twice betrayed David's hiding place to Saul, and where David wrote of trust betrayed.
BiblicalSignificance: Ziph is the town that sold David to Saul, and the wilderness where he learned to trust God over men.

Name: Zoan
Description: An ancient capital of Egypt, older than Hebron by seven years according to Numbers, and the place of God's wonders in the psalms.
BiblicalSignificance: Zoan is Egypt's ancient capital, where the wonders of the exodus are remembered.

Name: Zoar
ModernLocation: Unknown; traditionally associated with the southeastern Dead Sea region
Description: The small city of the plain, also called Bela, to which Lot fled and which was spared at his plea.
BiblicalSignificance: Zoar is the city spared for one man's sake: Lot's refuge when Sodom burned, and the ancestor-city of Moab and Ammon's line.

Name: Zobah
Description: An Aramean kingdom that warred with Saul and David, and whose king Hadadezer David defeated. Its exact place is not stated.
BiblicalSignificance: Zobah is the Aramean power David broke on his way to empire.

Name: Zorah
Description: A Danite town in the Shephelah, home of Manoah and birthplace of Samson, near Eshtaol.
BiblicalSignificance: Zorah is Samson's hometown, where the angel appeared to Manoah and his wife.

Name: Baal-zephon
Description: The Exodus station named as the landmark opposite which Israel camped before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before the Red Sea crossing. The Egyptians overtook Israel encamped there by the sea. The location of Baal-zephon is unknown, and no modern site is claimed for it here.
BiblicalSignificance: Baal-zephon marks the place where Israel, camped with the sea before them and Pharaoh's army behind them, waited for the deliverance only God could bring.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea

Name: Beth-jeshimoth
Description: A Moabite town on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, where Israel made its last camp east of the Jordan, pitching from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim before crossing into the promised land. It later appears among the towns allotted to Reuben and among the frontier cities of Moab named in Ezekiel's oracle. Its modern site is commonly proposed as Tell el-Azeimeh in Jordan.
BiblicalSignificance: Beth-jeshimoth marks the threshold of the promised land: Israel's last camp before the Jordan crossing, and later a frontier town on Moab's border.

Name: Brook Kanah
Description: The brook that formed part of the boundary between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh in the division of the land west of the Jordan. Joshua 16 describes it on Ephraim's border, and Joshua 17 describes it again on the border between Ephraim to the south and Manasseh to the north. Wadi Qana is the standard identification of the brook, stated here as such.
BiblicalSignificance: Kanah matters because boundaries mattered. In a land given by lot and inheritance, a brook line between brother tribes kept each family's portion clear and kept peace between Ephraim and Manasseh, the two sons of Joseph. The brook is a reminder that the conquest ended not only in battles won but in an ordered, shared inheritance.

Name: Brook Zered
Description: The brook or valley that Israel crossed on the way from Kadesh toward the land of Moab, marking the border of Moab. Deuteronomy says the crossing came after thirty-eight years, when the generation of the men of war had passed away from the camp, so that the wandering generation's time in the wilderness was over. Wadi el-Hasa in Jordan is the commonly accepted identification of the brook; it is stated here as the standard identification, not as certain.
BiblicalSignificance: Zered is a quiet turning point: a stream crossed, and a generation gone. Israel's long wandering ends not with a battle but with a boundary crossed, as the people God had disciplined step toward the land their children would enter. The brook also marks the edge of Moab, land Israel was told not to take, so the crossing is as much about obedience to God's limits as it is about progress.

Name: Gath-hepher
Description: A town in Zebulun, on the border described in Joshua (where the KJV spells it Gittah-hepher), and the hometown of Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet whose word Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders fulfilled. Its modern site is traditionally identified with el-Meshhed in Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: Gath-hepher is remembered as Jonah's hometown, tying the prophet of Nineveh to a small Galilean town and to God's word about Israel's borders.

Name: Geba
Description: A Benjaminite city, identified with Jaba' in the West Bank, where Jonathan struck down the Philistine garrison, sparking open war with the Philistines. It was later given to the Levites as one of their cities, and under Josiah it marked the northern end of his reform, 'from Geba to Beer-sheba,' when he defiled the high places.
BiblicalSignificance: Geba shows how one bold act of faith can change the course of a war, and how a place of battle later became a place set apart for the Levites' service.

Name: Gerasa
Description: A city of the Decapolis east of the Jordan, in the region where Jesus cast out the legion of demons and sent them into a herd of swine. The naming of this region varies in the Gospel manuscripts: the on-site KJV reads 'the country of the Gadarenes' in Mark 5:1 and 'the country of the Gergesenes' in Matthew 8:28, while Gerasa is the Decapolis city named in the variant tradition for the same region and event. The healed man was told to tell his friends what the Lord had done for him, and he published it throughout Decapolis.
BiblicalSignificance: Gerasa is where Jesus' power over the demonic was displayed in Gentile territory, and where a healed outcast became the region's first witness.

Name: Greece
Description: The land of Hellas, the Greek world whose people profile is the Greece entry in Ancient Civilizations, as distinct from its parts: the existing Achaia and Macedonia place entries are Roman-era regions within this larger land, not the whole of it. In Daniel, Greece appears in prophecy as the kingdom that would follow Persia, with its king named as the king of Grecia, and in Zechariah its sons stand for the Greek world opposed to God's people. By the time of Acts, Greece was the world Paul travelled through, preaching in its cities. This entry is the land as a whole, across both Testaments, rather than any one Greek city or province.
BiblicalSignificance: Greece matters in Scripture chiefly as the power that shaped the world between the Testaments: Daniel foresaw its empire, the Hellenistic age that followed spread the Greek language in which the New Testament was written, and Paul carried the gospel through its cities.

Name: Kirioth
Description: A Moabite city named in the oracles of judgment against Moab: Jeremiah lists it among the cities of Moab, far and near, declares that Kerioth is taken, and Amos warns that fire will devour its palaces. The KJV spells the name Kerioth in these passages. Its location is uncertain, and no modern site is claimed for it here. It is distinct from Kerioth in Judah (Joshua 15:25), a minor town in the south of Judah that is not the Moabite city of these oracles.
BiblicalSignificance: Kirioth stands among the proud cities of Moab that the prophets warned would fall, a reminder that no city is beyond God's judgment.

Name: Land of Israel
Description: The land of the united and divided kingdoms as a whole, whose people profile is the Israel entry in Ancient Civilizations, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south. The overlap is stated honestly: Canaan, already a place entry, is the same land under its pre-conquest name, and Judaea and Galilee, already place entries, are its later parts, in the south and the north respectively; this entry is the kingdom-era whole, not a replacement for any of them. Samuel's phrase from Dan even to Beersheba became the standard way of describing the whole land, and Solomon's reign is described as all Israel dwelling safely from Dan even to Beersheba.
BiblicalSignificance: The Land of Israel as a whole is the stage of the monarchy: one kingdom under Saul, David and Solomon, then divided, yet still spoken of as a single land from Dan to Beersheba.
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; Building of Solomon's Temple; The Kingdom Divides

Name: Land of the Hittites
Description: The Anatolian territory of the Hittite Empire, whose people profile is the Hittite Empire entry in Ancient Civilizations, with its capital at Hattusa. This entry is the LAND, not the people: the Hittite Empire civilization entry describes the people and their empire, while this entry describes their homeland in central Anatolia. It is also not the existing Cappadocia place entry, which is a later Roman province in the same broad area, not the Bronze Age Hittite homeland. In Scripture the land of the Hittites marks the northern extent of the land promised to Israel, and Hittite kings traded with Solomon in horses and chariots.
BiblicalSignificance: The land of the Hittites shows how far the promised land's description stretched in Joshua, to a great empire far beyond Israel's borders, and how Hittites remained neighbours and trading partners of Israel from the patriarchs to Solomon.

Name: Michmash
Description: A Benjaminite town, identified with Mukhmas in the West Bank, where the Philistines encamped against Israel and where Jonathan and his armor-bearer routed them, beginning a pursuit that carried the battle from Michmash to Aijalon. Isaiah later names Michmash on the Assyrian army's march toward Jerusalem, where it laid up its carriages.
BiblicalSignificance: Michmash is where a two-man act of trust in God turned into a rout of a far larger army, showing that the battle belongs to the Lord.

Name: Ophir
Description: The gold land of Solomon's voyages, reached by ships sent with Hiram's servants, which brought back gold, almug trees, and precious stones, and whose gold became a byword for wealth. Ophir is also named in the Table of Nations as a son of Joktan, and Job pictures a man laying his gold in the dust, even the gold of Ophir. No modern location is given here, because Ophir's location is debated: Arabia, India, and Africa have all been proposed, and none is asserted here as settled.
BiblicalSignificance: Ophir is Scripture's picture of wealth at its most distant and dazzling, gold that had to be sailed for and waited three years to return. Solomon's Ophir voyages mark the height of his kingdom's reach and riches, the same riches that the prophets and wisdom writers would later warn could not buy what God alone gives. Job's use of Ophir gold makes the point plainly: even the finest gold of the farthest land is dust beside submission to God.
RelatedPeople: Joktan; King Solomon; Hiram, King of Tyre

Name: Perea
ModernLocation: East bank of the Jordan Valley, northwestern Jordan (general)
Description: The region east of the Jordan where Jesus ministered, described in the Gospels as the country 'beyond Jordan': great multitudes followed him there, and he returned there to the place where John had first baptized. 'Perea' itself is the post-biblical, Josephus-era name for this region; it is not a word the King James Version uses, and the Gospels speak of the place simply as beyond Jordan.
BiblicalSignificance: Perea shows that Jesus' ministry was not confined to Galilee and Jerusalem. Crowds from beyond Jordan followed him, he taught and healed there, and after conflict in Jerusalem he withdrew again to the place of John's baptizing, where many believed on him. The region east of the river thus belongs to the heart of his public ministry, not to its margins.

Name: Petra
Description: The later Nabataean rock city in Jordan, traditionally identified with the Sela of 2 Kings 14:7, which Amaziah took by war and called Joktheel, and of Isaiah 16:1, where the lamb is sent to the ruler of the land from Sela. That identification of Petra with biblical Sela is debated, and the existing Sela entry likewise presents it only as traditional; this entry therefore carries the identification as traditional, not settled. Petra itself is not named in Scripture.
BiblicalSignificance: Petra, if it is biblical Sela, is the rock city taken by Amaziah and named in Isaiah's message to Moab; as a traditional identification, it is presented here with that debate stated openly.

Name: River Ahava
Description: A river or canal in Babylonia where Ezra gathered the returning exiles on their way back to Jerusalem. There Ezra proclaimed a fast, that the company might humble themselves before God and seek a safe journey for themselves, their children, and their goods. The exact canal is unidentified, and this entry does not guess at its course or modern course.
BiblicalSignificance: Ahava is where the return from exile paused for prayer before it moved. Ezra would not ask the king for soldiers and horsemen; instead the exiles fasted and sought God's protection for the road, and God answered. The gathering at Ahava also exposed a practical problem for the journey: no Levites were found among those assembled, and Ezra sent for ministers for the house of God before setting out.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Name: Tarshish
Description: A distant maritime land, reached by ships, famous for its trade: the ships of Tarshish brought Solomon gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks, and the kings of Tarshish are pictured bringing presents to the king. Jonah fled toward Tarshish when God sent him to Nineveh, boarding a ship at Joppa to get as far from his calling as the sea would take him. No modern location is given here, because Tarshish's location is debated: Tartessos in Spain is commonly proposed, while Sardinia and Tarsus have also been proposed, and none is asserted here as settled.
BiblicalSignificance: Tarshish stands in Scripture for the far edge of the known world, the place you go when you want to be out of reach. Jonah chose it precisely because it was far from Nineveh and, as he imagined, far from the LORD's presence, yet the storm found him on the way and the fish brought him back. At the same time Tarshish's ships and tribute point to a world wider than Israel, whose distant kings would one day bring gifts to God's king.

Name: Territory of Asher
ModernLocation: Northwestern Israel and southern Lebanon, along the Mediterranean coast
Description: The tribe takes its name from Asher, son of Jacob and Zilpah, Leah's servant (Genesis 30:13; 49:20). The coastal allotment of the tribe Asher, whose people profile is the Asher entry in Ancient Civilizations, in the far north-west of the land, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:24-31. Its border ran along the Mediterranean coast, reaching toward Sidon in the north and touching the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali inland; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include the coastal cities Sidon and Tyre. The tribe did not drive out all the inhabitants of its allotment, and in Judges Asher is noted as dwelling among the Canaanites.
BiblicalSignificance: Asher's allotment shows the conquest as inheritance with unfinished work: land given by lot, yet neighbours left in place, setting up the compromises Judges describes.
RelatedPeople: Asher; Serah; Beriah; Heber; Anna the Prophetess

Name: Territory of Benjamin
Description: The tribe takes its name from Benjamin, son of Jacob and Rachel, who died bearing him (Genesis 35:16-18). The allotment of the tribe Benjamin, whose people profile is the Benjamin entry in Ancient Civilizations, lying between Judah to the south and Ephraim to the north, as described in general terms in Joshua 18:11-28. Its border ran from the Jordan valley in the east, through the central hill country, toward the western approaches; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Jericho, Gibeon, Ramah and Mizpah, with Jerusalem on its southern border. In Judges, Benjamin's story continues in the civil war of Judges 19-21, after which the tribe survived greatly reduced.
BiblicalSignificance: Benjamin's small central allotment became a hinge between north and south: it held Jerusalem's border, produced Israel's first king, and nearly vanished in civil war before being restored.
RelatedPeople: Benjamin; King Saul; Jonathan; Ehud, Son of Gera; Mordecai; Queen Esther; Paul; Kish, Son of Abiel

Name: Territory of Dan
Description: The tribe takes its name from Dan, son of Jacob and Bilhah, Rachel's servant (Genesis 30:6; 49:16-17). The original allotment of the tribe Dan, whose people profile is the Dan entry in Ancient Civilizations, on the coastal plain west of Benjamin and Ephraim, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:40-48. This entry is the TERRITORY, not the city: the existing Dan place entry is the CITY in the far north, the place the tribe renamed Dan after capturing Laish. Joshua gives the territory's boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key city among existing place entries is Joppa, on its coastal edge. Finding its original allotment too hard to hold, part of the tribe later migrated north to Laish, which it renamed Dan, so the tribe's name came to mark Israel's northern edge as well as its original coastal home.
BiblicalSignificance: Dan's territory tells two stories at once: an allotment on the coast that the tribe could not hold, and a migration north that gave Israel its proverbial northern boundary, from Dan to Beersheba.
RelatedPeople: Dan; Samson; Manoah, Father of Samson; Aholiab

Name: Territory of Ephraim
ModernLocation: Central Israel, in the hill country north of Benjamin
Description: The tribe takes its name from Ephraim, son of Joseph, adopted by Jacob as a full tribal ancestor (Genesis 41:52; 48:5, 14). The hill-country allotment of the tribe Ephraim, whose people profile is the Ephraim entry in Ancient Civilizations, lying between Benjamin to the south and Manasseh to the north, as described in general terms in Joshua 16:5-10. Its border ran from the Jordan valley in the east across the central hills toward the Mediterranean coast in the west; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Shechem, Shiloh and Bethel. In Judges, Ephraim appears as a proud and prominent tribe, disputing with Gideon and later with Jephthah.
BiblicalSignificance: Ephraim's central hill country held the tabernacle at Shiloh and the covenant gathering place at Shechem, and later gave its name to the northern kingdom as a whole.
RelatedPeople: Ephraim; Joshua; Jeroboam; Abdon, Son of Hillel; Samuel; Deborah

Name: Territory of Gad
ModernLocation: Jordan, east of the Jordan River in the Gilead region
Description: The tribe takes its name from Gad, son of Jacob and Zilpah, Leah's servant (Genesis 30:11; 49:19). The Transjordan allotment of the tribe Gad, whose people profile is the Gad entry in Ancient Civilizations, east of the Jordan River, as described in general terms in Joshua 13:24-28. Its territory lay in the Gilead region, between Reuben to the south and the eastern half of Manasseh to the north, with the Jordan valley as its western edge; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Ramoth-gilead, Mahanaim and Jazer. Gad was one of the tribes that settled east of the Jordan before the rest of Israel crossed over, on condition that its fighting men would help conquer the land west of the river.
BiblicalSignificance: Gad's Transjordan home shows Israel's inheritance reaching beyond the Jordan itself, and the tension that came with it: settled early, yet expected to fight alongside its brothers for land it would not itself occupy.
RelatedPeople: Gad; Heber, Son of Gad's House

Name: Territory of Issachar
ModernLocation: Northern Israel, in the Jezreel Valley
Description: The tribe takes its name from Issachar, son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 30:18; 49:14-15). The allotment of the tribe Issachar, whose people profile is the Issachar entry in Ancient Civilizations, in the fertile Jezreel Valley region of the north, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:17-23. Its territory lay between Zebulun to the west, Naphtali to the north and Manasseh to the south, with the Jordan valley to its east; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key city among existing place entries is Jezreel, in the valley that bears its name. In Judges, the princes of Issachar stood with Deborah and Barak against Sisera.
BiblicalSignificance: Issachar's valley allotment put the tribe on a great east-west route through the land, and its leaders are remembered in Deborah's song as standing with Israel in battle.
RelatedPeople: Issachar; Tola, Son of Puah; Baasha, King of Israel

Name: Territory of Judah
ModernLocation: Southern Israel, in the southern hill country
Description: The tribe takes its name from Judah, son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:35; 49:8-10). The large southern allotment of the tribe Judah, whose people profile is the Judah entry in Ancient Civilizations, as described in general terms in Joshua 15:1-63. Its border ran from the Dead Sea and the southern wilderness in the south and east, across the southern hill country, to the Mediterranean coast in the west, with Benjamin to its north; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Jerusalem, Hebron, Bethlehem and Beersheba. This entry is the Joshua allotment, not the later region: the existing Judaea place entry is the later Roman-era region covering the south in the time of Christ. Simeon's allotment lay inside Judah's territory. Judah later became the southern kingdom, and the tribe from which David and, in the New Testament, Jesus came.
BiblicalSignificance: Judah's allotment became the heartland of the southern kingdom and of David's dynasty, holding Jerusalem, Hebron and Bethlehem within a single tribal inheritance.
RelatedPeople: Judah; King David; King Solomon; Rehoboam; King Asa; King Jehoshaphat; King Hezekiah; King Josiah; Zerubbabel; Caleb; Boaz; Jesse; Othniel, Son of Kenaz; Amos; Micah

Name: Territory of Manasseh
ModernLocation: Northern Israel and Jordan, on both sides of the Jordan River
Description: The tribe takes its name from Manasseh, son of Joseph, adopted by Jacob as a full tribal ancestor (Genesis 41:51; 48:5, 14). The allotment of the tribe Manasseh, whose people profile is the Manasseh entry in Ancient Civilizations, divided between two half-tribes on opposite sides of the Jordan, as described in general terms in Joshua 13:29-31 and Joshua 17:1-13. The eastern half lay in the Transjordan, in the Bashan region north of Gad, and the western half lay in the northern hill country and coastal plain west of the Jordan, between Ephraim to the south and Issachar and Asher to the north; Joshua gives its boundaries by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by precise surveyed lines, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Bethshan and Megiddo. In Judges, Manasseh's story continues with Gideon, who was of Manasseh.
BiblicalSignificance: Manasseh is the only tribe with an inheritance on both sides of the Jordan, a reminder that the promise was never confined to one bank of the river, and its western towns long remained partly unconquered.
RelatedPeople: Manasseh; Gideon; Jephthah, Judge of Israel; Jair, the Gileadite; Zelophehad

Name: Territory of Naphtali
ModernLocation: Northern Israel, in the Galilee region
Description: The tribe takes its name from Naphtali, son of Jacob and Bilhah, Rachel's servant (Genesis 30:8; 49:21). The northern allotment of the tribe Naphtali, whose people profile is the Naphtali entry in Ancient Civilizations, in the hill country of the far north, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:32-39. Its territory lay between Asher to the west, Zebulun and Issachar to the south, and the upper Jordan valley to the east; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include the fortified cities Hazor and Kedesh. In Judges, Barak of Naphtali led Israel's army with Deborah against Sisera.
BiblicalSignificance: Naphtali's northern hill country guarded Israel's frontier toward Syria, and its people are remembered in Deborah's song as risking their lives on the heights of the battlefield.

Name: Territory of Reuben
ModernLocation: Jordan, east of the Dead Sea and the lower Jordan River
Description: The tribe takes its name from Reuben, son of Jacob and Leah, Jacob's firstborn (Genesis 29:32; 49:3-4). The southernmost Transjordan allotment of the tribe Reuben, whose people profile is the Reuben entry in Ancient Civilizations, east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, as described in general terms in Joshua 13:15-23. Its territory lay south of Gad, with the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley as its western edge, reaching south toward Moab; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. Its key cities among existing place entries include Heshbon, Dibon, Aroer and Medeba. Like Gad, Reuben settled east of the Jordan before the crossing, on condition that its fighting men would help conquer the land west of the river. In Judges, Reuben is noted for staying among the sheepfolds while other tribes went to war.
BiblicalSignificance: Reuben, the firstborn's tribe, settled first and furthest east, and its later hesitation in Judges stands in contrast to the urgency of its original bargain to fight for its brothers.

Name: Territory of Simeon
ModernLocation: Southern Israel, within the territory of Judah, around Beersheba
Description: The tribe takes its name from Simeon, son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:33; 49:5-7). The allotment of the tribe Simeon, whose people profile is the Simeon entry in Ancient Civilizations, lying inside Judah's larger allotment in the south, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:1-9. Joshua states expressly that Simeon's inheritance was taken from within Judah's portion, because Judah's share was too large for it; no precise border is claimed here, since Joshua gives the allotment by named towns within Judah's territory. Its key city among existing place entries is Beersheba, in the southern Negev. In Judges, Simeon joined with Judah in the early fighting to take possession of the land.
BiblicalSignificance: Simeon is the tribe without a territory of its own apart from Judah: its inheritance inside another tribe's land foreshadows its gradual absorption into Judah in later history.
RelatedPeople: Simeon; Zimri, Son of Salu; Shaul

Name: Territory of Zebulun
ModernLocation: Northern Israel, in the Lower Galilee
Description: The tribe takes its name from Zebulun, son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 30:20; 49:13). The allotment of the tribe Zebulun, whose people profile is the Zebulun entry in Ancient Civilizations, in the Lower Galilee of the north, as described in general terms in Joshua 19:10-16. Its territory lay between Asher to the west, Naphtali to the north and Issachar to the south-east, reaching toward Mount Tabor; Joshua gives its boundary by neighbouring territories and named towns, not by a precise surveyed line, and no precise border is claimed here. None of the towns named in its Joshua allotment yet has a separate place entry on the site, so no key city is claimed here rather than naming one that is not an existing entry. In Judges, Zebulun is praised for risking its life in the battle against Sisera.
BiblicalSignificance: Zebulun's small Galilean allotment, tucked between larger neighbours, is remembered not for size but for courage: its people jeoparded their lives unto death in Deborah's battle.

Name: Valley of Salt
Description: The valley where David's forces defeated Edom and where Amaziah, king of Judah, later slew ten thousand Edomites. The title of Psalm 60 associates that psalm with the same campaign, when Joab returned and smote Edom in the valley of salt. The valley's location is debated and is left blank here: the Arabah south of the Dead Sea is commonly proposed, but that identification is not asserted as settled.
BiblicalSignificance: The Valley of Salt is remembered as a place of hard-won victory over Edom, first under David and again under Amaziah, and it gave David a name for his fame in war. Yet the psalm tied to the campaign is also a prayer of a people who felt cast off and broken, asking God to turn to them again. Victory and dependence sit side by side: the battle was won, and the victory still had to be prayed for.

Name: Valley of Shaveh
Description: The King's Valley where the king of Sodom met Abram after Abram had rescued Lot and defeated the kings who had taken him. Abram came home from the battle with captives and goods recovered, and the meeting in the valley set the stage for his encounter with Melchizedek, king of Salem. The valley's location is uncertain and is left blank here; it is traditionally associated with the area near Salem, or Jerusalem, but that tradition is not asserted as certain.
BiblicalSignificance: Shaveh is the valley of homecoming after rescue. Abram had risked everything for his nephew Lot, and the king of Sodom came out to meet the victor in the King's Valley, offering a bargain over persons and goods. What follows in the chapter matters more than the bargain: Abram meets Melchizedek, is blessed, and refuses to be enriched by Sodom, so that no one could say a king of Sodom had made Abram rich.

Name: Wilderness of Shur
ModernLocation: Northwestern Sinai / Egypt's eastern borderland (approximate, general)
Description: The desert east of Egypt, on Egypt's eastern borderland, where Hagar fled from Sarah and was found by the angel of the LORD at a fountain in the way to Shur, and where Israel entered after crossing the Red Sea and went three days finding no water. The same wilderness later marked the edge of Saul's campaign against Amalek and of David's raids. Its modern placement is given only in general, approximate terms: the northwestern Sinai and Egypt's eastern borderland.
BiblicalSignificance: Shur is the wilderness of both flight and first steps. Hagar, alone and fleeing, met God there and was told to return, with a promise about the son she carried. Israel, newly delivered, walked into the same desert and within three days was thirsty, learning that freedom still meant daily dependence on God for water. Shur therefore stands at the start of the wilderness story in both generations: a place where God meets people who have nowhere else to go.
RelatedPeople: Hagar; Moses; King Saul; King David
RelatedEvents: Hagar and Ishmael; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Name: Wilderness of Sinai
Description: The desert around Mount Sinai where Israel camped after leaving Rephidim, where the LORD gave the Law, and where the people were numbered and ordered for the march to Canaan. This entry is distinct from the existing Mount Sinai place entry: the wilderness is the desert region of the encampment, not the mountain itself. No modern location is given here, because the location of Sinai itself is debated among scholars, so the wilderness around it cannot be fixed with confidence either.
BiblicalSignificance: The Wilderness of Sinai is where Israel stopped wandering and became a covenant nation. At Sinai they heard the Ten Commandments, received the pattern of the tabernacle, failed with the golden calf, and were forgiven and reordered. The census in Numbers was taken here, and from here the cloud lifted and the march began. Sinai is less a dot on a map than the place where a rescued people were given God's law and identity.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Golden Calf
